meta.blurb: Richard Hannay has a dead neighbour in his flat, a notebook full of code and strangers watching his door. The police will blame him. So he borrows a milkman's coat and runs for Scotland, with a spy gang close behind.
meta.bible: Richard Hannay: a Scottish-born mining engineer, home from Rhodesia, brave, practical and quick-witted; the hero. Scudder: an American neighbour in Hannay's building who knows of a plot; he is found dead. Karolides: the Greek prime minister, due to visit London on 15 June. The Black Stone: a secret group of German spies working to steal British war plans. The Professor: the bald, polite leader of the Black Stone, whose eyelids close like a hawk's. Sir Harry: a young politician in Scotland who hides Hannay. Sir Walter Bullivant: a senior official at the Foreign Office. Inspector Scaife: a Scotland Yard detective. Royer: a French general who visits London for the secret meeting. Trafalgar Lodge: the villains' house on the Kent coast near Bradgate; thirty-nine steps lead from it down to the sea. Ariadne: the spies' yacht, due at high tide at seventeen minutes past ten in the evening. Galloway: the wild moorland of south-west Scotland. Rhodesia, London, Scotland, Scotland Yard, Foreign Office, Kent, Germany, France, Britain, Africa, American, Greek, German, French. Portland Place: the London street where Hannay has his flat and Scudder is killed. The milkman: lends Hannay his white coat, cap and cans for a gold coin. The literary innkeeper: a tall, kind, book-loving innkeeper in Galloway who asks no questions. Sir Harry: a young politician who hosts a village meeting, mistakes Hannay for the expected speaker, then believes his story and lends him clothes. The roadmender: an old man in round spectacles who breaks stones by the road and watches Hannay's boots; he works for the Black Stone. The aeroplane: a small plane that searches the moor for Hannay. The Professor's house: a lonely house at the end of a track on the moor where Hannay is locked in a room and blows the door open with blasting explosive. The fisherman: a quiet stranger who feeds Hannay and lends him money; the date is then 12 June. Scudder's cipher: the notebook says Karolides is a decoy and the real prize is the plans drawn up at the secret meeting on 15 June; it also says thirty-nine steps and high tide at seventeen minutes past ten. Sir Walter's country house is in the south of England; Hannay arrives on the night of 13 June. The old naval officer: a retired officer, friend of Sir Walter, who names Trafalgar Lodge at Bradgate. Scaife arrests the three men on the lawn; the Professor says he serves Germany. Sarajevo: on 28 June 1914 the heir to the Austrian throne is shot there. On 4 August 1914 Britain declares war on Germany and Hannay joins the army. The white house papers: copies of the plans and lists of agents are found in Trafalgar Lodge. Voice and tone: fast, plain and tense, a chase told with dry humour; a death is stated plainly with no gore; Hannay tells the story as a man who is not a hero by trade.

beats.scene: A tall man in a travelling coat steps off a ship into grey drizzle
beats.summary: Richard Hannay, a mining engineer, arrives in London from Rhodesia in the spring of 1914.

beats.scene: Hannay looks into shop windows on a wide, busy London street
beats.summary: Hannay spends his first weeks in London buying clothes and seeing the sights, and is soon tired of them.

beats.scene: Hannay sits at a long club table among men in evening dress
beats.summary: At dinners and clubs, people talk only of small things, and Hannay finds them tiresome.

beats.scene: Men in a smoking room read newspapers beside a glowing fire
beats.summary: The newspapers speak of trouble in Europe, but the men at the club say there will be no war.

beats.scene: Hannay walks alone along a crowded pavement among pale, hurrying faces
beats.summary: Hannay finds the London crowds pale and hurried and misses the open sky of Africa.

beats.scene: Hannay marks a calendar at his desk beside a pile of unread letters
beats.summary: Hannay decides that if nothing interesting happens, he will return to Africa at the end of the month.

beats.scene: Hannay walks home along a quiet street in the long May dusk
beats.summary: After dinner at his club, Hannay walks home through the long, soft dusk of a May evening.

beats.scene: Hannay lights a pipe by an open window in his sitting room
beats.summary: Back at his flat in Portland Place, Hannay lights a pipe and thinks of the African veldt.

beats.scene: Hannay studies a printed list of ships under a reading lamp
beats.summary: Hannay looks at the sailing lists and plans to visit the shipping office in the morning.

beats.scene: A thin man with bright eyes stands in the lamp-lit doorway
beats.summary: A knock at the door brings Hannay face to face with Scudder, a thin, nervous man from the same building.

beats.scene: A nervous man bolts a door and peers behind a curtain
beats.summary: Scudder asks to come in, bolts the door behind him and checks the street from behind the curtain.

beats.scene: Scudder drinks whisky with a shaking hand in a lamp-lit sitting room
beats.summary: Scudder asks for whisky and drinks it quickly; his hand shakes, but his eyes are sharp.

beats.scene: Scudder sits forward in an armchair and studies Hannay's face
beats.summary: Scudder asks whether Hannay can keep a secret and says he chose him because he is new to London.

beats.scene: Scudder whispers urgently while Hannay frowns at him from across the lamp
beats.summary: Scudder says he will be a dead man within days unless Hannay helps him; Hannay thinks about the police.

beats.scene: A man in a shabby coat counts papers beside a window at night
beats.summary: Scudder says he is an American who has spent years listening in the cafes and hotels of Europe.

beats.scene: Scudder holds up one finger as he speaks in a darkened room
beats.summary: Scudder says that the great wars of the world are not accidents but are planned by small hidden groups.

beats.scene: Scudder taps a name on a folded newspaper with a trembling finger
beats.summary: Scudder says that Karolides, the Greek prime minister, will be killed in London on 15 June.

beats.scene: A map of Europe lies on a table with small crosses marked on it
beats.summary: Scudder explains that a killing in London would set the great powers against each other like a spark in dry straw.

beats.scene: Hannay leans back and frowns, unsure whether to believe his visitor
beats.summary: Hannay thinks the story sounds like a tall tale, yet he cannot ignore the real fear in Scudder's face.

beats.scene: Scudder takes a small black notebook from his coat and holds it up
beats.summary: Scudder shows Hannay a small black notebook full of numbers and says that everything is written in it.

beats.scene: Scudder whispers a name while shadows from the lamp fall across his face
beats.summary: Scudder says the plotters call themselves the Black Stone and that they will kill anyone who knows their secret.

beats.scene: A drawing of a bird of prey with half-closed eyes lies on a table
beats.summary: Scudder describes the leader of the Black Stone, an old man whose eyelids close over his eyes like a hawk's.

beats.scene: Scudder rubs his tired face and stares at the floor
beats.summary: Scudder explains that he learned the group's secret too well, and that they discovered him listening.

beats.scene: Scudder peers from a window at a figure in a doorway
beats.summary: Scudder says that he has moved from place to place and thinks the Black Stone has found him again.

beats.scene: Hannay studies the thin brown face in the lamplight and slowly nods
beats.summary: Hannay looks at the frightened man, thinks of his dull weeks, and decides to believe him.

beats.scene: Hannay opens the door of a small, tidy spare room
beats.summary: Hannay offers his spare room, and Scudder accepts and asks him to tell no one.

beats.scene: Scudder writes at a small table in the spare room with a candle
beats.summary: Scudder asks for paper and pens and settles in the spare room to put his notes in order.

beats.scene: Hannay lies awake in bed listening to a pen scratching through the wall
beats.summary: Hannay lies awake, hearing the scratch of a pen and the footsteps in the street outside.

beats.scene: Scudder drinks tea at a breakfast table, calmer in the morning light
beats.summary: In the morning Scudder is calmer and says he knows a man in high office who can stop the plot.

beats.scene: Scudder presses a small black notebook into Hannay's hand at the door
beats.summary: That evening Hannay goes out to dine, and Scudder presses the notebook into his hand to keep.

beats.scene: Hannay climbs a dark staircase and puts a key in a door at midnight
beats.summary: Hannay comes home late, finds the flat dark and silent, and calls out for Scudder without an answer.

beats.scene: A man lies on the sitting room floor beside an overturned chair
beats.summary: Hannay finds Scudder dead on the sitting room floor with a long knife through his heart.

beats.scene: A clock ticks on a mantelpiece above a still figure on the carpet
beats.summary: Hannay stands numb with shock while the clock on the mantelpiece goes on ticking calmly.

beats.scene: Drawers hang open and papers lie scattered across a ransacked spare room
beats.summary: Hannay sees that the flat has been searched and realises that the killers were looking for the notebook.

beats.scene: Hannay sits in the dark with his head in his hands beside a lamp
beats.summary: Hannay realises that the police will think he is the murderer, because he is the dead man's only friend.

beats.scene: A man crouches by a curtain looking down at a night street
beats.summary: Hannay peers through the curtain and sees two men standing in the street, watching the door of the building.

beats.scene: A railway guide lies open beside a candle and a small black notebook
beats.summary: Hannay studies a railway guide and decides to hide in the wildest part of Scotland he can find.

beats.scene: A milk can clinks on a stone step outside a door before dawn
beats.summary: Before dawn Hannay hears the milkman's boots on the stairs and has an idea.

beats.scene: Hannay hands a gold coin to a grinning milkman in the stairwell
beats.summary: Hannay offers the milkman a coin for his cap and coat, saying it is a joke on some friends below.

beats.scene: A man in a white coat and flat cap steps out into dawn
beats.summary: Dressed as the milkman, Hannay takes the cans and steps out of the building into the dawn.

beats.scene: A man in a white coat carries cans past two men
beats.summary: Hannay walks down the street with his cans, passing close to the two watchers.

beats.scene: A watcher in a bowler hat glances at a milkman and turns away
beats.summary: One watcher looks at him for a moment but sees only a tired milkman and turns back to the door.

beats.scene: A discarded white coat and two milk cans sit on a quiet doorstep
beats.summary: Round the corner Hannay takes off the coat and leaves it folded with the cans where the milkman can find it.

beats.scene: A busy railway station at dawn with a huge board of departing trains
beats.summary: At a great railway station Hannay buys a ticket for a small station in the wild south-west of Scotland.

beats.scene: A steam train pulls out of a London station, Hannay at a window
beats.summary: The train pulls out of London, and Hannay sits in the corner of a carriage and breathes again.

beats.scene: Green fields and white clouds roll past a train window in morning light
beats.summary: Hour after hour the fields roll past while Hannay thinks about Scudder and the notebook.

beats.scene: A newsboy holds up an evening paper on a crowded railway platform
beats.summary: At a big station Hannay buys an evening paper and reads of a murder in Portland Place.

beats.scene: A talkative traveller in tweed chats beside a silent man in the corner
beats.summary: A talkative passenger says that the murderer will be caught soon, while Hannay hides behind his newspaper.

beats.scene: A small train winds through grey hills at dusk on a lonely branch line
beats.summary: As evening comes Hannay changes to a slow branch line that wanders into empty country.

beats.scene: A lone traveller steps down onto a tiny platform lit by one lamp
beats.summary: At last Hannay steps down at a tiny station in Galloway, where the air smells of heather and peat smoke.

beats.scene: A lone traveller climbs a dark hillside under a sky full of stars
beats.summary: Hannay walks out of the station into the dark, climbs onto the moor and sleeps beside a stone wall.

beats.scene: Sunrise spreads gold across a wide brown moor with larks in the sky
beats.summary: Hannay wakes at dawn to the song of larks and sees a huge, empty country of brown hills and silver lochs.

beats.scene: Hannay counts a few coins and a handful of biscuits on a flat stone
beats.summary: Hannay counts his money and food and decides to avoid towns and live quietly until the fifteenth of June.

beats.scene: A shepherd and two black-and-white dogs stand on a green hillside
beats.summary: Hannay meets a shepherd and his dogs, says he is on a walking holiday and hears of an inn a few miles away.

beats.scene: A small stone cottage with a broken door stands beside a stream
beats.summary: Hannay finds an empty shepherd's cottage beside a stream and decides to rest there until night.

beats.scene: A candle burns on a bare table beside an open black notebook
beats.summary: By candlelight Hannay opens the black notebook and finds page after page of numbers.

beats.scene: A finger follows a few plain words among the numbers on a page
beats.summary: Among the numbers Hannay finds a few words written plainly: names, dates and the strange phrase thirty-nine steps.

beats.scene: Hannay frowns over a sheet of paper covered with small calculations
beats.summary: Hannay guesses that the numbers are a cipher built on a keyword, and he tries one word after another.

beats.scene: Hannay sits upright as a line of figures turns into letters on paper
beats.summary: At last, as grey light creeps through the window, the key fits and the numbers begin to turn into letters.

beats.scene: Hannay stares at the first decoded sentence on a scrap of paper
beats.summary: The first decoded words show that the plot to kill Karolides is only part of something much bigger.

beats.scene: A candle flickers over neat handwriting on a sheet of paper
beats.summary: Scudder's notes say that the Black Stone are German agents who are working to carry secrets out of Britain.

beats.scene: A newspaper headline about a Greek statesman lies beside a candle
beats.summary: The notes say that the plan to kill Karolides is a decoy to make the world look the wrong way.

beats.scene: A French general in a blue uniform shakes hands with a tall British officer
beats.summary: On 15 June a French general named Royer is to meet British leaders in secret to settle how their navies will work together.

beats.scene: A shadowy figure copies a document by lamplight in a small room
beats.summary: The Black Stone has learned the date and the place, and it means to copy the plans once the meeting is over.

beats.scene: A boat with a single lantern rides on a dark swell near a cliff
beats.summary: To get the plans out of Britain the spies will use a boat at high tide, and Scudder notes thirty-nine steps and the time.

beats.scene: Hannay stares up at a tall stone tower with a winding staircase
beats.summary: Hannay wonders what thirty-nine steps can mean and thinks of stairs in towers, churches and hotels.

beats.scene: A finger rests on a name at the foot of a handwritten page
beats.summary: The last page names Bullivant at the Foreign Office as the one man who can stop the plot.

beats.scene: A hunted man stares at the wall of an empty cottage
beats.summary: Hannay sees that he cannot walk into the Foreign Office as a wanted man, and he does not even know where Bullivant lives.

beats.scene: Hannay ties a small black notebook inside his shirt with a piece of string
beats.summary: Hannay ties the notebook inside his shirt, burns his rough notes and keeps the key to the code in his head.

beats.scene: A thin wisp of smoke rises from a chimney in a far, dim valley
beats.summary: At dusk, after a long day's walk over the moors, Hannay sees a light in the distance and heads for the inn.

beats.scene: A small stone inn with one lit window beside a moor
beats.summary: Hannay reaches a small stone inn in a valley and knocks at the door.

beats.scene: A tall, stooping man with kind eyes opens a door with a lamp
beats.summary: The innkeeper, a tall, stooping man with kind eyes, welcomes the dusty traveller and asks no questions.

beats.scene: A traveller eats eggs, bacon and oatcakes at a scrubbed kitchen table
beats.summary: Hannay eats a huge supper of eggs, bacon and oatcakes in the warm kitchen.

beats.scene: Shelves crowded with worn books surround a smiling innkeeper by the fire
beats.summary: The innkeeper shows Hannay his shelves of books and says that his great love is a good story.

beats.scene: Hannay gestures with both hands as an innkeeper listens, wide-eyed
beats.summary: Hannay, who must say something, tells a story of his years in Africa, and the innkeeper listens with delight.

beats.scene: A folded newspaper on a chair shows a headline about a murder in London
beats.summary: Hannay notices an old newspaper on a chair that carries a headline about the Portland Place murder.

beats.scene: An innkeeper taps a newspaper and smiles slyly at a tired guest
beats.summary: The innkeeper says that he follows murders as a hobby and thinks the police are fools; Hannay agrees as calmly as he can.

beats.scene: A narrow bed under a sloping ceiling in a plain upstairs room
beats.summary: Hannay goes up to a small room under the roof and sleeps with the notebook still tied to his chest.

beats.scene: Headlamps sweep across a bedroom ceiling as a motor engine stops
beats.summary: In the middle of the night Hannay wakes to the sound of a motor car, and lamps sweep across the ceiling.

beats.scene: Hannay crouches at the top of a dark stair listening to voices below
beats.summary: Hannay creeps to the top of the stairs and hears two strangers asking the innkeeper about a man who looks like him.

beats.scene: A man climbs from a small window onto a shed roof
beats.summary: Hannay climbs out of the window onto a shed roof, drops to the yard and leaves a coin on the sill.

beats.scene: A man lies flat in a ditch as headlamps sweep past
beats.summary: Hannay hides in a ditch as the car with the two strangers goes slowly past, searching the road with its lamps.

beats.scene: A tired man in muddy clothes walks along a misty country road at dawn
beats.summary: At dawn Hannay, wet, muddy and hungry, follows a road down towards a village.

beats.scene: A poster pinned to a wall announces a meeting in the village hall
beats.summary: In the village Hannay buys bread and sees a poster for a political meeting in the hall that evening.

beats.scene: A tired man sleeps in a sunny corner of a field behind a hedge
beats.summary: Hannay eats his bread in a quiet field, sleeps through the day and walks back along the road in the evening.

beats.scene: A young man in a car leans out and waves at a stranger
beats.summary: A young man in a car calls out to Hannay, mistakes him for the speaker the village has been waiting for, and begs him to hurry.

beats.scene: Two men in a car with bright lamps follow a village road at dusk
beats.summary: Far down the road Hannay sees the headlamps of the strangers' car, and he decides that a crowded hall is the safest place to hide.

beats.scene: A village hall packed with farmers under hanging lamps and a platform
beats.summary: Inside the packed hall Hannay is led to a platform and shaken by the hand by the young chairman, Sir Harry.

beats.scene: Two strangers stand at the back of a crowded hall
beats.summary: At the back of the hall Hannay sees the two strangers slip in, scanning every face, and lowers his head.

beats.scene: Sir Harry presents a tall stranger to a cheering hall
beats.summary: Sir Harry introduces Hannay as the guest from London, and the crowd cheers as he rises to speak.

beats.scene: Hannay stands at the front of a platform and clears his throat
beats.summary: Hannay begins nervously, saying that he knows little of politics but a good deal about hard work and open country.

beats.scene: A tall man speaks to rows of listening faces under hanging lamps
beats.summary: Hannay warns the crowd that nations can drift towards trouble like sleepers walking towards a cliff.

beats.scene: Farmers laugh and slap their knees as Hannay waves one hand
beats.summary: Hannay mixes in a few jokes from his years in Africa, and the farmers laugh and cheer.

beats.scene: A man sits down to wild applause while a chairman beams
beats.summary: Hannay sits down at last to loud applause, and Sir Harry whispers that it was the best speech of the campaign.

beats.scene: A car with bright headlamps drives away from a village hall at night
beats.summary: The two strangers have gone from the back of the hall, and Hannay hears a car drive off down the road.

beats.scene: Two men walk together along a dark village lane towards a large house
beats.summary: After the meeting Sir Harry takes Hannay home to his house and thanks him for saving the evening.

beats.scene: Two men sit by a dying fire late at night in a book-lined study
beats.summary: Late at night by the fire, Hannay decides to trust Sir Harry and tells him the whole truth.

beats.scene: A young man stares into the fire with a serious face
beats.summary: Sir Harry listens in silence to the whole tale, then says quietly that he believes every word of it.

beats.scene: Sir Harry unfolds a letter and points to a name on the page
beats.summary: Sir Harry says that he knows Sir Walter Bullivant and will write to him, while Hannay waits out of sight.

beats.scene: Clothes and a small car wait in a misty yard at dawn
beats.summary: In the morning Sir Harry gives Hannay a bundle of clothes and promises that the police will hear nothing.

beats.scene: Two men shake hands beside a small car at a lonely crossroads
beats.summary: Sir Harry drops Hannay at a lonely crossroads and says that he will write to Sir Walter at once.

beats.scene: A man in a tweed jacket and cap walks along a sunny country road
beats.summary: In his borrowed tweed clothes Hannay feels safer, and he walks the sunny road enjoying the birds and the warmth.

beats.scene: An old man in round spectacles breaks stones beside a country road
beats.summary: Hannay meets an old man in spectacles who is breaking stones at the roadside, and they talk about the weather.

beats.scene: A spectacled man looks down at a pair of boots on a dusty road
beats.summary: The old man looks at Hannay's boots for rather too long and says that they are fine boots for a farm hand.

beats.scene: A sharp pair of eyes watches a man through round spectacles
beats.summary: The old man asks where Hannay has come from, and behind his spectacles his eyes look sharp and wide awake.

beats.scene: A man on a hillside looks back at a figure watching from the road
beats.summary: As Hannay walks away he looks back and sees the old man standing still, watching him, with his spectacles in his hand.

beats.scene: A small aeroplane flies low over green hills against a bright sky
beats.summary: From the top of the hill Hannay hears a strange humming and sees a small aeroplane flying low over the moor.

beats.scene: A man lies flat in the heather while an aeroplane circles above him
beats.summary: The aeroplane turns and circles over Hannay as if it is looking for something, and he drops flat in the heather.

beats.scene: A man crawls through bracken beside a stream as a plane passes overhead
beats.summary: Hannay crawls through bracken to a stream and lies hidden while the aeroplane passes twice above him.

beats.scene: An aeroplane lands on a flat green hillside while men run towards it
beats.summary: The aeroplane drops lower, lands on a flat stretch of moor a mile away, and Hannay sees two men hurry towards it.

beats.scene: Two men search a hillside with sticks while an aeroplane waits nearby
beats.summary: The men from the aeroplane search the hillside for Hannay, who lies still beside the stream until they give up.

beats.scene: An aeroplane lifts into a darkening sky above a quiet moor
beats.summary: At sunset the aeroplane rises into the sky and flies away to the east, and Hannay breathes again.

beats.scene: A man walks across a dark moor under a sky full of stars
beats.summary: Hannay leaves the road and walks south across the moor by the stars, keeping far from any track.

beats.scene: A man pulls his leg out of a black bog as the moon rises
beats.summary: In the dark Hannay falls into a bog up to his knees and drags himself out, tired, wet and very hungry.

beats.scene: A single yellow window shines in the dark at a track's end
beats.summary: Near midnight Hannay sees a single lit window at the end of a track, and he finds a lonely house behind a wall.

beats.scene: A bald old gentleman in a velvet jacket holds a door open and smiles
beats.summary: A gentle, bald old gentleman opens the door, sees the muddy traveller and invites him in with great kindness.

beats.scene: Roman coins and broken pottery lie on shelves in a warm study
beats.summary: In a warm study full of old coins and pottery, the old gentleman says that he is a collector of ancient things.

beats.scene: Hannay sits across a table from a smiling host, telling a careful story
beats.summary: Hannay tells the old gentleman a careful story about a walking holiday, leaving out London and the murder.

beats.scene: Headlamps shine through a window as a car stops outside a lonely house
beats.summary: A motor car arrives, and two of the old gentleman's friends come in, a tall man and a pale young man.

beats.scene: An old man's eyelids close slowly like a hawk's in the lamplight
beats.summary: As the old man turns in the lamplight, his eyelids slide slowly across his eyes like a hawk's, and Hannay knows him.

beats.scene: Two men seize a tall man by the arms in a lamp-lit study
beats.summary: The tall man and the young man seize Hannay, and the old gentleman says politely that they will talk in the morning.

beats.scene: A hand turns out the pockets of a muddy coat on a table
beats.summary: The men empty Hannay's pockets and find only a few coins, and in their hurry they do not open his shirt.

beats.scene: A key turns in the lock of a small bare room
beats.summary: Hannay is marched upstairs and locked in a small bare room with a shuttered window and a cupboard.

beats.scene: A man lies with his ear on the floorboards listening to voices below
beats.summary: Through the floor Hannay hears the men planning to leave at dawn and to deal with him before they go.

beats.scene: A man opens a tall cupboard and finds wooden boxes on a shelf
beats.summary: Hannay searches the room and finds in the cupboard a box of blasting explosive, fuses and detonators.

beats.scene: A man studies a stick of explosive in a shaft of moonlight
beats.summary: As a mining engineer, Hannay knows exactly what he holds, and he thinks of the daring plan that it makes possible.

beats.scene: A man packs a small charge against the hinge of a heavy door
beats.summary: Hannay builds a small charge against the door by the lock, fits a fuse and builds a shield from the bed.

beats.scene: A man crouches behind a bed as a fuse glows red
beats.summary: When the house is silent and the guard's steps have faded, Hannay lights the fuse and crouches behind the bed.

beats.scene: A heavy door blows off its hinges in a cloud of smoke and flame
beats.summary: The charge explodes with a roar that shakes the house, and the door is blown off its hinges in a cloud of smoke.

beats.scene: A man runs through a smoky passage and down a dark staircase
beats.summary: Hannay leaps through the smoke, runs down the stairs past the shouting men and bursts out of a back door into the garden.

beats.scene: A man runs across a dark moor with a red glow behind him
beats.summary: Hannay runs across the moor in the dark while a red glow rises behind him where the house has caught fire.

beats.scene: A man kneels to drink from a clear stream in a quiet glen
beats.summary: Parched with thirst, Hannay follows a stream down a glen, drinks from it and finds a man fishing in a pool.

beats.scene: A fisherman pours hot tea from a flask for a ragged traveller
beats.summary: The fisherman sees how tired and hungry Hannay is, and shares his sandwiches and a flask of hot tea.

beats.scene: A folded newspaper lies on a stone beside a fishing basket
beats.summary: While Hannay eats he sees a newspaper in the basket and reads with a shock that it is the twelfth of June.

beats.scene: A man stares at a distant road with a look of firm decision
beats.summary: Hannay decides that he cannot wait for a letter any longer, and he remembers where Sir Harry said that Sir Walter lives.

beats.scene: A small old motor car stands in a country lane beside a hedge
beats.summary: The fisherman offers to drive Hannay to the town station in his old motor car, and Hannay gratefully accepts.

beats.scene: A kind stranger counts banknotes into the hand of a muddy traveller
beats.summary: At the station the fisherman guesses Hannay has no money, lends him a few pounds without question, and wishes him good luck.

beats.scene: A night train rushes south through dark fields with lit carriage windows
beats.summary: Hannay takes a night train south, wedges himself into a corner, and sleeps and dreams of Scudder.

beats.scene: A traveller walks down a winding lane between high hedges in the evening
beats.summary: Hannay leaves the train at a small English station and walks the quiet lanes towards the village, with the evening sun behind him.

beats.scene: A tall wooden door at the end of a gravel drive in the dark
beats.summary: At night Hannay reaches Sir Walter Bullivant's house, a grand home at the end of a long drive, and knocks at the tall door.

beats.scene: A stiff butler looks down at a muddy stranger on a lamp-lit doorstep
beats.summary: A butler looks coldly at the muddy stranger, and Hannay says that he brings a message from Scudder.

beats.scene: A grey-haired man rises from a desk under a green-shaded lamp
beats.summary: The butler leads Hannay through a hall of portraits to a quiet study, where grey-haired Sir Walter rises from his desk.

beats.scene: A tall man in muddy clothes stands before a desk with open hands
beats.summary: Hannay gives his name and says that he did not kill Scudder, and Sir Walter quietly asks him to sit down.

beats.scene: A seated man tells a story while a grey-haired listener makes notes
beats.summary: Hannay tells the whole story from beginning to end while Sir Walter listens without a word and makes notes.

beats.scene: A small black notebook lies on a desk beside a green lamp
beats.summary: Hannay unties the notebook from his chest and lays it on the desk, and Sir Walter picks it up as if it were made of glass.

beats.scene: An older man bows his head over a desk in a silent study
beats.summary: Sir Walter says that Scudder worked for him and was one of his best men, and he is silent for a long time.

beats.scene: Sir Walter looks up with a steady gaze at the man across the desk
beats.summary: Sir Walter says that he believes Hannay, since the story matches what Scudder had been reporting for months.

beats.scene: Sir Walter spreads out a map of the Channel on a large desk
beats.summary: Sir Walter says that the real danger is not to Karolides but to the secret plans of Britain's navy.

beats.scene: A silver tray with food and a hot bath waiting in a warm bedroom
beats.summary: Sir Walter promises that Hannay is safe in his house and orders hot water, food and clean clothes.

beats.scene: A clean bed with white sheets under a lamp in a quiet bedroom
beats.summary: Hannay sleeps in a real bed, while Sir Walter locks the notebook in a safe and sits up reading it.

beats.scene: Maps and papers lie in tidy heaps on a desk in a smoky study
beats.summary: In the morning Sir Walter tells Hannay that he has sent for help and that the meeting will take place tomorrow.

beats.scene: A grey-haired man frowns over a telegram beside an open window
beats.summary: A telegram says that Karolides has arrived safely under guard, and Sir Walter says that Hannay must stay hidden at the house.

beats.scene: Two men bend over a small black notebook under a green lamp
beats.summary: Sir Walter and Hannay study the notebook together and try to guess what the thirty-nine steps can be.

beats.scene: A grey-haired man in a travelling coat steps into a waiting motor car
beats.summary: Sir Walter leaves for London to see that the meeting is properly guarded, and tells Hannay to rest and wait.

beats.scene: A man walks restlessly along a gravel path in a walled garden
beats.summary: Hannay cannot sleep or read, and he walks restlessly round the garden, thinking over the clues.

beats.scene: A French general shakes hands with British officers in a large quiet room
beats.summary: In London a French general shakes hands with British leaders, and the secret meeting begins and ends without trouble.

beats.scene: A grey-haired man steps out of a car and looks worried and tired
beats.summary: Sir Walter returns in the late afternoon with news that the meeting went perfectly, but Hannay is not comforted.

beats.scene: Hannay looks at a clock on a mantelpiece showing late afternoon
beats.summary: Hannay says that if the spies have copied the plans, they will leave tonight by boat at seventeen minutes past ten.

beats.scene: Heavy books and tide tables are spread across a library table
beats.summary: Sir Walter and Hannay search the library for tide tables, and Sir Walter finds a book of the tides on the south coast.

beats.scene: A finger runs down a column of figures in a tide table
beats.summary: Running his finger down the table for 15 June, Hannay finds that high water at one place on the Kent coast is at seventeen minutes past ten.

beats.scene: A footman hurries down a drive towards a waiting motor car at dusk
beats.summary: Sir Walter sends a car to fetch an old naval officer who lives nearby and knows the coast of Kent.

beats.scene: A white-whiskered old officer strides into a library with a stick
beats.summary: The old naval officer arrives, listens eagerly and says that he knows Bradgate well.

beats.scene: A finger traces a coast on a map beside a cluster of small houses
beats.summary: He says that Bradgate is a small place with a few villas on a high cliff, and he names one called Trafalgar Lodge.

beats.scene: Hannay leans forward with a look of sudden excitement across a table
beats.summary: At the word stair Hannay leaps up, certain that the thirty-nine steps are the steps of Trafalgar Lodge.

beats.scene: A grey-haired man speaks into a telephone with a stern face
beats.summary: Sir Walter telephones Scotland Yard and asks for Inspector Scaife to come at once with a few trusted men.

beats.scene: A broad man in a bowler hat enters a hall and offers his hand
beats.summary: Inspector Scaife arrives within the hour, looks hard at Hannay and then shakes his hand.

beats.scene: A detective listens with folded arms while a tall man talks quickly
beats.summary: Scaife listens to the story and says that it explains things that had puzzled him, including the milkman's tale.

beats.scene: Policemen in plain coats climb into two dark cars in a country drive
beats.summary: Scaife says that they must catch the spies in the act and sets off with six plain-clothes men in two cars.

beats.scene: A motor car races along an empty country lane as the sun sets red
beats.summary: The cars race through country lanes as the evening comes, Sir Walter watching the clock and urging them to hurry.

beats.scene: A white house on a high cliff above a calm grey sea
beats.summary: As the light fades they reach Bradgate, and Hannay sees Trafalgar Lodge, a white house on a high cliff above the sea.

beats.scene: Policemen creep along a dark lane beside a high hedge at dusk
beats.summary: Scaife places his men quietly in the lanes and leads Hannay along a hedge towards the garden of Trafalgar Lodge.

beats.scene: Three men in white play tennis on a lawn above a darkening sea
beats.summary: Through the hedge they see three men in white playing tennis on the lawn as calmly as holidaymakers.

beats.scene: A detective whispers to a tall man behind a hedge with a doubtful look
beats.summary: Scaife whispers that these men look like ordinary gentlemen, and asks Hannay whether he can be sure.

beats.scene: A man in white flannels walks towards a hedge to fetch a ball
beats.summary: A ball flies into the hedge, and one of the players walks over to fetch it, so close that Hannay could touch him.

beats.scene: An old man's calm eyes close slowly in the last light of evening
beats.summary: As the player straightens, his eyelids slide slowly across his eyes, and Hannay knows him for the bald old man of the moor.

beats.scene: Hannay whispers into a detective's ear as the tennis game continues
beats.summary: Hannay whispers to Scaife that this is the leader, and Scaife nods, but says they must wait until the boat comes.

beats.scene: Policemen take up positions at the corners of a garden in the dusk
beats.summary: Scaife sends his men quietly to the garden gates and the side of the house, while Hannay slips round to find the cliff stair.

beats.scene: A wooden stair clings to a chalk cliff above a dark beach
beats.summary: At the edge of the cliff Hannay finds a long wooden stair that goes down to the beach, and he begins to climb down.

beats.scene: A man counts wooden steps in the dark on a steep cliff stair
beats.summary: Counting aloud under his breath, Hannay goes down the stair and finds that it has exactly thirty-nine steps.

beats.scene: A white yacht rests at anchor in a dark bay under the stars
beats.summary: From the beach Hannay sees a white yacht at anchor in the bay and reads its name, Ariadne, in the starlight.

beats.scene: A man climbs a wooden stair at night with a hand on the rail
beats.summary: Hannay climbs back up the stair and whispers to Scaife that the steps are real and that the yacht is waiting.

beats.scene: Three men in dark coats walk from a lit house across a dim lawn
beats.summary: The three men stop playing, go into the house, and later come out in dark coats, one carrying a small leather case.

beats.scene: Small waves slap at a shingle beach under a sky full of stars
beats.summary: The sound of the waves grows louder as the tide rises, and the watchers crouch in the dark and wait.

beats.scene: A faint light moves over dark water towards a shingle beach
beats.summary: Far below, a faint light moves over the water towards the beach, and Hannay hears the creak of oars.

beats.scene: Three men hurry across a lawn in the dark towards a cliff stair
beats.summary: The three men walk swiftly across the lawn towards the stair, passing within a few feet of the hidden police.

beats.scene: A police whistle shrills as officers rush from the shadows of a garden
beats.summary: As the three men reach the stair, Scaife blows his whistle, and the policemen spring out from the shadows.

beats.scene: A bald old man stands stiff and silent between two officers in a garden
beats.summary: The younger men struggle and shout, but the old man stands stiff and silent, and the leather case falls to the grass.

beats.scene: An inspector speaks to a calm old man by lantern light
beats.summary: Scaife arrests the three men, and the old man quietly says that he is no archaeologist but a servant of his own country.

beats.scene: Policemen and coastguards crouch on a dark beach beside a landing boat
beats.summary: On the beach the yacht's boat grounds, and policemen and coastguards seize the sailors before they can row away.

beats.scene: A patrol boat with a searchlight stops a white yacht
beats.summary: Out in the bay a patrol boat shines a searchlight on the Ariadne and stops her from sailing away.

beats.scene: Policemen search a book-lined study with lanterns in a white house
beats.summary: Scaife and Sir Walter search the white house and find a study with papers laid out on the desk.

beats.scene: A grey-haired man compares two sheets of paper under a green lamp
beats.summary: In the leather case and the desk Sir Walter finds the copied plans, and he checks them with the greatest care.

beats.scene: A stack of coded letters and lists of names lies in an open drawer
beats.summary: The Black Stone's own papers, with names, codes and addresses, show how far the plot reached across Britain.

beats.scene: A grey-haired man grips the hand of a tall man on a dark lawn
beats.summary: Sir Walter shakes Hannay's hand on the lawn and says that Scudder would be proud of what he has done.

beats.scene: A man lays a gold coin in a grinning milkman's hand
beats.summary: Scotland Yard clears Hannay's name, and back in London he finds the milkman and gives him another gold coin.

beats.scene: Men stand with bowed heads beside a grave in a churchyard
beats.summary: Sir Walter arranges for Scudder to be buried with honour, and Hannay stands with a few quiet men beside the grave.

beats.scene: A newspaper headline on a dim street announces trouble in a distant city
beats.summary: On the twenty-eighth of June the heir to the Austrian throne is shot in Sarajevo, and Europe begins to slide towards war.

beats.scene: Newspaper headlines announce war on a wall of a crowded London street
beats.summary: On the fourth of August Britain declares war, and crowds fill the London streets while the newspapers shout the news.

beats.scene: A tall man in a new uniform stands before a recruiting officer's desk
beats.summary: Hannay goes to join the army, and his old boredom is gone for ever, since he has a purpose now.

beats.scene: A tall man on a cliff stair looks out over the sea
beats.summary: Before he leaves for training, Hannay visits Trafalgar Lodge cliff once more and looks back on the adventure that began with a knock.

A1A2: Richard Hannay came home from Africa in the spring of 1914.
He bought new clothes and visited the famous places of the city.
At dinner the men talked about small things, and he felt bored.
The newspapers wrote about trouble in Europe, but nobody worried.
The people in the street looked pale and tired and always in a hurry.
He told himself he would go back to Africa if nothing happened.
That night he walked home slowly through the soft evening light.
At home he lit his pipe and thought about the African hills.
He read the ship list and chose a day to leave.
Then someone knocked, and a thin man stood at the door.
Scudder came in, locked the door and looked at the street.
Scudder asked for whisky, and his hand shook as he drank.
He asked Hannay if he could keep a secret.
He said he would be dead in a few days.
Scudder said he came from America and had travelled in Europe for years.
He said that some men were planning a great war.
He said that a Greek leader would die in London on 15 June.
Scudder said a killing in London would start a big war.
Hannay thought the story was strange, but Scudder looked afraid.
Scudder took out a small black notebook full of numbers.
He said the men called themselves the Black Stone.
He said their leader was an old man with strange eyes.
Scudder had learned their secret, and they had found out.
He moved often, but he thought the men had found him.
Hannay looked at him and decided to believe the story.
Hannay gave him the small spare room and a key.
Scudder asked for paper and pens and began to write.
Hannay lay awake and heard the pen scratching through the wall.
In the morning he was calm and ate a good breakfast.
Scudder gave him the notebook and asked him to keep it.
Hannay came home late, but the flat was dark and silent.
He found Scudder dead on the floor of the sitting room.
Hannay stood still while the clock on the wall ticked.
The killers had searched the flat for something.
Hannay knew the police would think that he was the killer.
Through the curtain he saw two men watching the street door.
He looked at a train book and thought of Scotland.
Before dawn he heard the man with the milk on the stairs.
He gave the man a coin and asked for his white coat.
In the white coat, Hannay stepped out into the early light.
He walked down the street and passed the two watching men.
One man looked at him, then looked away again.
Round the corner he took off the coat and left it.
At the station he bought a ticket for a train to Scotland.
The train left London, and Hannay felt safer at last.
The fields went by while Hannay thought about Scudder.
He bought a newspaper and read about the murder.
A man in the train said the killer would soon be caught.
At dusk he changed to a slow train in empty country.
At last he got off at a tiny station in Galloway.
He walked into the dark and slept beside a stone wall.
He woke to the song of birds and saw empty hills.
He counted his money and food and made a plan.
A shepherd told him about an inn a few miles away.
He found an empty hut beside a stream and rested there.
At night he opened the notebook by the light of a candle.
A few words in the notebook were plain, like Karolides.
He thought the numbers were a code and tried many words.
At dawn the key fitted, and the numbers became words.
The first line said that the killing was only a trick.
Scudder wrote that the Black Stone worked for Germany.
Karolides was only a trick to make people look away.
On 15 June a French general would visit London in secret.
The Black Stone knew about the meeting and wanted the plans.
The spies planned to leave by boat at high tide.
Hannay wondered what the thirty-nine steps could be.
At the end Scudder wrote the name of a man named Bullivant.
Hannay could not walk into the Foreign Office as a wanted man.
Hannay hid the notebook inside his shirt and burned his notes.
After a long walk he saw a light and went toward it.
Hannay reached the little inn and knocked at the door.
A tall kind man opened the door and asked him in.
In the warm kitchen Hannay ate eggs, bacon and bread.
The man loved books and showed Hannay his shelves.
Hannay told a story about Africa, and the man listened.
On a chair he saw a newspaper about the London murder.
The man said the police were fools, and Hannay agreed.
Hannay went upstairs and slept with the notebook on him.
In the night he woke to the sound of a motor car.
He went quietly to the stairs and heard two strangers talking.
He climbed out of the window and dropped into the yard.
He hid in a ditch while the car drove slowly past.
At dawn he walked along a road toward a village.
In the village he saw a paper about a meeting.
He ate, slept in a field and walked back at evening.
A young man thought he was the man who would speak.
Down the road he saw the strangers' car coming.
The hall was full, and a man named Sir Harry welcomed him.
At the back of the hall two strangers looked at every face.
Sir Harry introduced Hannay, and the crowd cheered loudly.
Hannay began to speak, but he felt very nervous.
He warned the people that a nation can walk into trouble.
He told a joke from Africa, and the farmers laughed.
He sat down, and the people clapped and shouted.
The two strangers were gone, and a car drove away.
After the meeting Sir Harry took Hannay to his big house.
By the fire Hannay decided to tell Sir Harry the truth.
Sir Harry listened quietly and then said that he believed him.
Sir Harry said he knew Sir Walter Bullivant of the Foreign Office.
In the morning Sir Harry gave Hannay clothes and a promise.
Sir Harry left Hannay at a crossroads and wished him luck.
In his new clothes he walked along the road and felt safer.
An old man was breaking stones by the road, and they talked.
The old man looked at his boots for a long time.
The old man asked him questions, and his eyes were sharp.
He walked away, but the old man was still watching him.
A small plane flew over the hills with a loud noise.
The plane flew in circles above him, and he lay down.
He crawled to a stream and hid while the plane passed.
The plane landed on the moor, and men hurried toward it.
The men searched the hill, but Hannay lay very still.
At sunset the plane flew away, and the hills were quiet.
He left the road and walked south under the stars.
He fell into a bog and pulled himself out.
Near midnight he saw a light at the end of a track.
A kind old man with a bald head opened the door.
The old man's study was full of old coins and pots.
Hannay told a simple story and left out the murder.
A car arrived, and two friends of the old man came in.
The old man's eyes closed like a bird's, and Hannay knew him.
The men seized Hannay, and the old man smiled politely.
They searched his pockets but did not open his shirt.
They locked Hannay in a small bare room upstairs.
Through the floor he heard the men talking about him.
In the cupboard he found a box of explosive stuff.
Hannay knew about explosives, and he made a plan.
He put a small charge against the door and added a fuse.
Hannay waited until the house was quiet, then lit the fuse.
The explosion blew the door off with a loud bang.
He ran down the stairs and out through the back door.
He ran across the moor while a red glow rose behind him.
He found a stream, drank, and saw a man fishing.
The fisherman gave him sandwiches and hot tea.
He saw a newspaper and learned it was the twelfth of June.
Hannay decided that he must go to Sir Walter at once.
The fisherman offered him a lift to the town station.
The fisherman lent him some money and wished him luck.
He took a night train south and slept in a corner.
He left the train and walked through quiet English lanes.
At night he reached a grand house and knocked.
A servant opened the door, and Hannay asked to see Sir Walter.
Hannay was led to a quiet room where Sir Walter sat.
Hannay said he did not kill Scudder, and Sir Walter nodded.
Hannay told his whole story, and Sir Walter wrote notes.
Hannay put the black notebook on the desk.
Sir Walter said Scudder had worked for his office.
Sir Walter said that he believed Hannay's story.
Sir Walter said the spies wanted the secret plans of the navy.
Sir Walter said Hannay was safe and gave him food.
Hannay slept in a real bed while Sir Walter read the book.
Next morning Sir Walter told Hannay about his plans.
A telegram said that Karolides was safe under guard.
Sir Walter and Hannay read the notebook and thought about the steps.
Sir Walter left for London and told Hannay to wait.
Hannay was restless and walked in the garden.
In London the secret meeting took place, and all went well.
Sir Walter came back and said that the meeting went well.
If the spies have the plans, they will leave tonight.
They looked for tide tables and found a book of the tides.
His finger stopped at the place where the tide was right.
Sir Walter sent a car to fetch an old friend from the navy.
The old naval officer came and said he knew Bradgate well.
He said a house called Trafalgar Lodge stood on the cliff.
At the word stair Hannay jumped up, full of hope.
Sir Walter called Scotland Yard and asked for Inspector Scaife.
Scaife arrived and shook Hannay's hand.
Scaife listened to the story and believed it.
Scaife said they must catch the spies in the act.
The cars raced through country lanes as the sun went down.
At dusk they saw a white house on a cliff above the sea.
Scaife put his men in the lanes and led Hannay to the house.
They saw three men in white playing tennis on the lawn.
Scaife whispered that the men looked quite ordinary.
A ball flew into the hedge, and one man came to get it.
The man's eyes closed slowly, and Hannay knew him.
Hannay whispered that this was the leader of the spies.
Scaife put men at the gates, and Hannay went to find the stair.
At the cliff Hannay found a long wooden stair and went down.
He counted the steps as he went down, and there were thirty-nine.
He saw a white yacht in the bay and read its name.
Hannay climbed back up and told Scaife about the steps.
The men stopped their game, went into the house and came out later.
The tide rose, and the waves grew louder in the dark.
A small light moved over the water, and he heard a boat.
The three men hurried across the lawn toward the stair.
Scaife blew his whistle, and the police ran out.
The young men shouted, but the old man stood still and silent.
Scaife arrested the men, and the old man admitted who he was.
On the beach the police caught the sailors from the yacht.
A patrol boat stopped the white yacht before she could sail.
The police searched the white house and found a study.
Sir Walter found the copied plans in the leather case.
They found the papers of the Black Stone, with many names.
Sir Walter shook Hannay's hand and thanked him.
In London Hannay found the man with the milk and gave him a coin.
Scudder was buried with honour, and Hannay stood by the grave.
In late June, news came of a killing in a far city.
On the fourth of August, Britain went to war.
Hannay went to join the army and felt no more boredom.
Hannay looked at the sea and remembered the adventure.
B1B2: Richard Hannay has worked for many years as a mining engineer in Rhodesia. In the spring of 1914 he steps off a ship in London, a city he has dreamed about for a long time.
For the first weeks Hannay is busy buying clothes, visiting the old streets and looking at the famous buildings. After a month, however, he finds that he has nothing left to do.
Hannay is invited to clubs and dinners where the guests talk only of horses, golf and their neighbours. He listens politely, but he cannot make himself care about any of it.
The newspapers are full of quarrels between the great powers of Europe, especially in the Balkans. Nobody at Hannay's club seems worried, and most people say that there will be no war.
Hannay watches the crowds hurrying along the pavements with pale faces and worried eyes. He thinks of the wide African sky, and he wonders why he ever wanted to leave it.
One evening in May Hannay makes up his mind about what to do next. If nothing interesting happens before the end of the month, he will take the next ship back to Africa.
On the evening of his decision Hannay dines alone at his club and then walks home. The sun has set, but the sky still holds a soft light.
At his flat in Portland Place, Hannay opens the window and lights his pipe. The noise of the street rises up to him, but his mind is far away in Africa.
Hannay takes down a list of ships sailing for Africa and studies the dates. He decides to go to the shipping office first thing in the morning and ask about a cabin.
Just then there is a knock at the door. Hannay opens it and finds a thin, brown-faced man with very bright eyes, who lives in the same building.
The man says that his name is Scudder and asks if he may come in. Once inside, he bolts the door and peers carefully through the curtain at the street below.
Scudder asks for a whisky and drinks it in two quick swallows. His hand is shaking, yet his eyes stay sharp and clear, and he does not look like a man who is drunk.
Scudder leans forward and asks whether Hannay is a man who can keep a secret. He explains that he has watched Hannay for days, and that he seems to be a stranger in London with no friends to talk.
Scudder says that within a few days he will be a dead man unless somebody helps him. Hannay suggests the police, but Scudder shakes his head and says that they would not believe him.
Scudder explains that he is an American who has travelled across Europe for years. He has sat in cafes and hotel lounges, listening to people who thought nobody was paying attention.

Scudder says that people think wars come by accident, but that is not always true. Somewhere in Europe, he whispers, a small group of hidden men has decided to start a great war and is making its plans.
Scudder names Karolides, the prime minister of Greece, who is coming to London on 15 June. He says that Karolides is going to be murdered while he is a guest in the city.
Scudder explains that a murder in London would shock the world. The great nations have promised to fight for each other, he says, and one spark would be enough to set them all on fire.
To Hannay the story sounds like the kind of tale that men tell after a long dinner. But the fear in Scudder's face is real, and it is hard to laugh at a man who is honestly frightened.
Scudder pulls a small black notebook from his coat and holds it up. The pages are covered with columns of numbers and strange signs, and he says that the whole story is written there.
Scudder says that the men behind the plot call themselves the Black Stone. They are patient and clever, he warns, and they will kill anyone who knows their secret.
Scudder describes the leader of the Black Stone as a calm, polite old man. His most unusual feature is his eyelids, which he can draw across his eyes sideways, like the eyelids of a hawk.

Scudder explains why the men of the Black Stone are hunting him so hard. He learned too much about their plans, and a fortnight ago they discovered him listening in a place where he should not have been.
Scudder says that he has changed his lodgings three times in two weeks. This afternoon he saw a man outside the building, and he is sure that the man is following him.
Hannay looks at Scudder's thin face for a long moment. He thinks of his empty weeks in London and decides that, true or false, this is the first interesting thing to happen to him.
Hannay offers Scudder the small spare room at the back of the flat. Scudder thanks him warmly, but he asks him to tell nobody, not even his friends, that he is there.
Before bed, Scudder asks for paper, ink and a good supply of pens. He takes the black notebook into the spare room, saying that he must put his notes in order before it is too late.
For a long time that night Hannay lies awake in the dark. Through the wall he can hear the steady scratch of Scudder's pen, and sometimes a man's footsteps pass slowly along the street outside.
In the morning Scudder looks calmer and eats a large breakfast. He tells Hannay that a man in high office can stop the plot, and that he will go to him very soon.
That evening Hannay puts on his coat to go out to dinner. At the door Scudder presses the black notebook into his hand and asks him to keep it safe.
Hannay returns long after midnight, tired but cheerful after an evening out. The flat is dark and silent, and when he calls out Scudder's name, nobody answers him.
Hannay lights a lamp and finds Scudder lying on the floor of the sitting room. A long knife has been driven through his heart, and he is quite dead.
For a few minutes Hannay cannot move or think. The clock on the mantelpiece goes on ticking calmly, as if nothing in the world has changed.

Hannay goes through the flat and sees that every drawer has been pulled open and every paper thrown on the floor. The killers were clearly looking for something, and he realises that it must be the notebook in his pocket.
Hannay sits down in the dark and tries hard to think clearly. A stranger is dead in his flat and nobody knew he was there, so the police will blame the man who lives in it.
Hannay creeps to the window and looks down through a gap in the curtain. Two men are standing in the street opposite, one beneath a lamp and one at the corner, and both are watching his door.
Hannay opens a railway guide and a map on the table, and he thinks about where a hunted man could hide. He decides on Scotland, where the hills are wide and empty and the police will look last.
Just before dawn Hannay hears the clink of cans and a whistling man coming up the stairs. It is the milkman on his daily round, and in a flash Hannay has an idea.
Hannay opens the door and offers the surprised milkman a gold coin. He explains that he wants to play a joke on some friends downstairs, and he would like to borrow the man's cap and coat.
Hannay puts on the milkman's cap and white coat and pulls the cap low over his eyes. Carrying two heavy cans, he walks down the stairs and steps out of the building into the grey light of dawn.
Hannay walks slowly down the street, swinging his cans as a working man would. He passes within a few steps of the two watchers, and his heart is beating so loudly that he thinks they must hear it.
One of the watchers glances at him, and for a moment Hannay's blood runs cold. Then the man sees nothing but a sleepy working man with milk cans, and he turns back to watch the door.
Round the corner, in a quiet side street, Hannay takes off the white coat and the cap. He folds them neatly beside the cans on a doorstep, where the milkman will be able to find them.

At a great railway station, Hannay reads the long board of departing trains. He buys a ticket for a small station in Galloway, because the village is so remote that nobody would think of looking for him there.
The train pulls out of the station, and the roofs of London slide slowly past the window. Hannay sits in the corner of a third-class carriage and breathes freely for the first time since midnight.
Hour after hour the green fields roll past the window while the wheels beat out a steady rhythm. Hannay thinks about Scudder, and he feels that he owes the dead man something that he must pay.
At a big station on the way north, Hannay buys an evening newspaper. It reports a murder in Portland Place, and the police say that they are anxious to find the man who rented the flat.
A talkative passenger in the carriage reads the news aloud and says that the murderer will certainly be caught. Hannay hides behind his newspaper and says that he hopes so too.
As the evening comes, Hannay changes at a junction to a slow little train on a branch line. It wanders through emptier and wilder country, and one by one the other passengers get off.
At last the train stops at a tiny station with one lamp and one porter. Hannay steps down, and the cool air smells of heather and peat smoke.
Hannay leaves the station and walks along a lane until the houses end. He climbs onto the open moor, finds a stone wall for shelter, and falls asleep among the heather under the stars.
Hannay wakes at dawn to the song of larks. Brown hills roll away under the pale sky, and small lochs shine like silver coins, but there is not a house to be seen.

Sitting on a flat stone, Hannay empties his pockets and counts what he has. He has little money, a few biscuits and the notebook, so he decides to avoid towns and stay hidden until the fifteenth of June.
In the morning Hannay meets a shepherd with two dogs. He says that he is on a walking holiday, and the shepherd tells him about a small inn a few miles to the east.
Instead of going to the inn at once, Hannay wanders on and finds an empty stone cottage beside a stream. It has a table, a bench and a roof, and he decides to rest there until it is dark.
When it is dark, Hannay lights a stub of candle that he found in the cottage. He opens the black notebook and sees page after page of numbers, written small and neat in Scudder's hand.
Here and there among the numbers Hannay finds a few words written plainly. He sees the names of people, some dates, and a strange phrase that he cannot understand, which is thirty-nine steps.
Hannay has seen simple codes before and guesses that these numbers stand for letters. If so, there must be a keyword, and for hours he tries one word after another without any success.
At last, as the grey light of morning creeps through the window, Hannay tries a name that Scudder had mentioned. It fits, and the numbers on the page begin to turn into letters.

The first sentences that Hannay manages to decode make him stare in surprise. They say that the plan to murder Karolides is only a trick, and that something far larger and more dangerous lies behind it.
Scudder's notes explain that the Black Stone are agents of Germany. Their real work is to find out British secrets and to carry them safely out of the country.
According to the notes, the plan to kill Karolides is a decoy. If the whole world is looking at Greece and the Balkans, nobody will notice what is really happening in London.
The notes say that on 15 June a French general named Royer will come secretly to London. He will meet British leaders, and together they will plan how their ships would fight side by side in a war.
Scudder writes that the Black Stone has learned about the meeting. Its agents intend to copy the secret plans as soon as the talks are over, and Hannay can see why the notes are so urgent.
Scudder believes that the spies will carry the plans out of England by boat, at night and at high tide. He writes only two clues, the words thirty-nine steps and the time, seventeen minutes past ten.

Hannay wonders for a long time what the thirty-nine steps can possibly be. He thinks of church towers, hotels and lighthouses, but a staircase could be anywhere, and the number is so exact that it must mean something.
At the foot of the last page Scudder has written a name. It is Bullivant, a senior man at the Foreign Office, and Scudder says that he is the one person who can stop the plot.
Hannay knows that he cannot simply walk into the Foreign Office. The police are looking for him, and he does not even know where Bullivant lives, only the name.
Hannay ties the notebook inside his shirt with a piece of string. He burns the paper with his rough notes and keeps the key to the code only in his head.
Hannay sleeps for a few hours and then walks all day over the moors, careful to stay away from the roads. At dusk he sees a light in a far valley, and he knows that it must be the inn.
The inn is a low stone building with one lit window and a sign that creaks in the wind. Hannay knocks at the door, and he hears slow footsteps coming across the floor inside.
The innkeeper is a tall, stooping man with kind eyes and a long grey moustache. He holds up a lamp, looks at the dusty stranger and invites him in without asking a single question.
In the warm kitchen the innkeeper puts a big supper before Hannay: eggs, bacon, oatcakes and hot tea. Hannay eats like a hungry wolf, and he pays for it in advance.
The kitchen walls are covered with shelves full of old books. The innkeeper says that he has read every adventure story he could find, and he loves a good tale more than a good dinner.
Hannay feels that he must pay for his supper with a story, so he tells a tale from his years in Africa. He leaves out the dangerous parts, and the innkeeper listens with shining eyes.
On a chair near the fire there is a folded newspaper from London. Hannay glances at it and sees, in thick black letters, a headline about the murder in Portland Place.
The innkeeper picks up the newspaper and says that he follows murders as a hobby. He says that a clever man would never be found by the police, and Hannay agrees as calmly as he can.
The innkeeper shows Hannay to a small room under the roof, with a narrow bed and a window over the road. Hannay lies down, with the notebook still tied to his chest, and soon he is asleep.
In the middle of the night Hannay wakes suddenly. The sound of a motor car comes up the road, its lamps sweep across the ceiling, and then the engine stops outside the inn.
Hannay creeps in his socks to the top of the stairs. Below him two strangers are asking the innkeeper about a tall, brown man with grey eyes who might have arrived that evening.
Hannay opens the window as quietly as he can and climbs onto the roof of a shed. He leaves a coin on the sill for the kind innkeeper, then drops lightly into the dark yard below.
Hannay runs across the fields and hides in a ditch beside the road. A little later the car with the two strangers comes slowly past, searching the hedges with its bright lamps.
At dawn Hannay is cold, wet and covered in mud. He follows a road down the hillside towards a village, and he knows that he looks like a man who slept in a ditch.
In the village Hannay buys bread and cheese from a small shop. On the wall outside there is a poster that announces a political meeting in the hall that evening, with a speaker from London.
Hannay eats his bread and cheese in a quiet field behind a hedge and sleeps for most of the day. In the evening, feeling much stronger, he walks back towards the road that leads to the village.
Just outside the village a young man in a small car stops beside Hannay. He cries out in relief, because he thinks that Hannay is the speaker from London who has been expected all evening.
Down the valley road Hannay sees the headlamps of a second car coming slowly closer. It is the car of the two strangers, and he decides that a crowded hall is the best place to hide.
The hall is packed with farmers in their best clothes. Hannay is led onto the platform, where the chairman, a young man called Sir Harry, shakes his hand warmly and looks hugely relieved.
As Sir Harry begins to introduce him, Hannay sees the two strangers slip in at the back of the hall. They stand with their hats in their hands, studying every face, and he lowers his head.
Sir Harry finishes his opening remarks and introduces his guest from London. The crowd cheers, and Hannay, feeling like a man who has stepped off a cliff, rises slowly to his feet.
Hannay begins in a nervous voice, and the whole hall waits quietly for him. He says that he knows little about politics but a great deal about hard work in wild country, and the farmers nod.

Hannay warns the crowd that nations can drift towards danger as a sleepwalker drifts towards the edge of a cliff. They are so busy with small quarrels, he says, that they do not see the big storm coming.
Hannay adds a few jokes from his time in Africa, and the farmers laugh and slap their knees. The more he says, the more the crowd likes him, and the louder the cheers become.
At last Hannay sits down, and the whole hall stands up to clap and shout. Sir Harry leans over and whispers that it was far better than the speech that he had been expecting.
The back of the hall is empty, because the two strangers have gone. Hannay hears the engine of a car start in the street, and he listens as the sound fades into the night.
When the hall has emptied, Sir Harry takes Hannay home to his large house on the hill. He explains that the real speaker never came, and he thanks Hannay for saving the evening.
Late at night, by the dying fire, Hannay studies the honest face of his host. He decides to trust him, and he tells him the whole story, from Scudder's first knock to the long walk across the moor.
Sir Harry listens without a single question from beginning to end. When Hannay has finished, he is silent for a long moment, and then he says quietly that he believes every word.
Sir Harry says that he knows Sir Walter Bullivant very well, since Sir Walter is an old friend of his family. He will write to him at once, and Hannay must wait out of sight until an answer comes.
In the morning mist Sir Harry hands Hannay a bundle of country clothes and an old cap. He promises that the police will hear nothing from him, and then he walks Hannay out to a waiting car.
Sir Harry drives Hannay to a lonely crossroads far from the village. He promises to write to Sir Walter at once, and they shake hands before the little car goes bumping away.
In his borrowed tweed jacket and old cap, Hannay looks like any farmer on his way to market. He feels safer than he has felt for days, and he enjoys the sunshine and the singing of the birds.
At a bend in the road Hannay comes across an old man in spectacles who is breaking stones with a hammer. He stops to chat about the weather, because it would seem strange to walk past without a word.
While they talk, the old man's eyes slide down to Hannay's boots and stay there for rather too long. He remarks slowly that they are very fine boots for a man in such old clothes.
The old man asks where Hannay is going and where he has come from. His voice is dull and sleepy, but behind the thick spectacles his eyes are sharp and wide awake, and Hannay does not like it.
As Hannay walks on up the hill, he looks back over his shoulder. The old man has stopped his work and is standing quite still, with his spectacles in his hand, watching him go.
From the top of the hill Hannay hears a strange humming in the sky. He looks up and sees a small aeroplane flying low over the moor, which is a rare sight in this part of the world.
The aeroplane turns and begins to circle slowly above the place where he stands. Hannay drops flat into the heather, because no pilot circles like that unless he is looking for something.

Hannay crawls through the heather to a stream and slides under the overhanging bracken. He lies there for a long time while the aeroplane passes twice above him, so low that he can hear the wires sing.
At last the aeroplane drops lower and lands on a flat green stretch of the moor, about a mile away. From the bracken Hannay sees two men hurry across the heather and climb in to talk to the pilot.
The men from the aeroplane search the hillside with sticks, beating the bracken and the heather. Hannay lies as still as a stone beside the stream, and at last the searchers give up and go back.

At sunset the aeroplane rises from the moor and flies away to the east, growing smaller and smaller. Hannay waits until the sound has quite died away, and then he crawls out of the bracken, stiff and cold.
Because the roads are no longer safe, Hannay strikes out across the open moor. He steers by the stars, keeping far away from every track, and his boots sink into the soft ground at almost every step.
In the dark Hannay steps into a hidden bog and sinks in up to his knees. He drags himself out at last, covered in black mud, and he is by now more tired and hungry than he has ever been.
Near midnight Hannay sees a yellow light shining in the distance. He follows it along a rough track and finds a large, lonely house standing behind a low stone wall.
A gentle, bald old gentleman in a velvet jacket opens the door. He sees the muddy, shivering traveller and cries that he must come in at once and have something to eat.
The old gentleman leads Hannay into a warm study full of ancient coins, broken pottery and rusty swords. He explains that his one passion is the study of the Roman past, and he brings bread and soup.
Over the soup the old gentleman asks where Hannay has come from, and Hannay tells him a careful story about a walking holiday. He says nothing of London, Scudder or the notebook under his shirt.
Soon afterwards a motor car draws up outside the house. Two friends of the old gentleman come in, a tall man and a pale young man, and they shake hands politely with Hannay.

As the old gentleman turns his head in the lamplight, his eyelids slide slowly across his eyes, exactly like a hawk's. Hannay's blood runs cold, because he knows at once that he has walked into the house of the Black Stone.

Before Hannay can move, the tall man and the young man seize him by the arms. The old gentleman smiles his gentle smile and says politely that they will talk in the morning, when everyone has had some rest.
The men turn out Hannay's pockets and find only a few coins and a knife. In their hurry they do not open his shirt, and the notebook stays tied against his chest.
Hannay is marched upstairs and pushed into a small bare room with a narrow window and a heavy shutter. The door slams, a key turns in the lock, and he hears the footsteps of a guard outside.
Hannay lies with his ear against the floorboards and can hear voices in the room below. The men are talking about leaving at dawn, and about what to do with him before they go.
Hannay searches the room in the dark and opens the tall cupboard. On the shelf, among some old tools, he finds a wooden box of blasting explosive, a roll of fuse and a handful of detonators.
As a mining engineer, Hannay knows exactly what he is holding. He studies the sticks in a shaft of moonlight, and slowly a daring plan takes shape in his mind.
Hannay builds a small charge and fixes it against the door beside the lock. He fits a fuse and a detonator, and then he drags the bed across the room to make a shield.
Hannay waits until the house is silent and the guard's footsteps have gone quiet at the far end of the passage. Then he lights the fuse, ducks behind the bed and covers his ears.
The charge explodes with a roar that shakes the whole house. The door is blown off its hinges in a cloud of smoke and splinters, and the sound of falling plaster rattles through the passage.
Hannay leaps through the smoke and runs along the passage, past the dazed guard, who is sitting on the floor. He rushes down the stairs, bursts out of a back door and races across the dark garden.
Hannay runs across the dark moor as fast as he can. Behind him a red glow is rising where a lamp has set the house alight, and shouting follows him for a long way.
Parched with thirst, Hannay follows a small stream down a green glen. He drinks the cold water, and a little farther on he finds a quiet man in a tweed hat who is fishing in a pool.
The fisherman takes one look at the ragged, muddy traveller and asks no questions. He shares his sandwiches and pours hot tea from a flask, and Hannay thinks that nothing has ever tasted so good.

Beside the fishing basket lies a newspaper that the fisherman has already read. Hannay glances at the date and feels a jolt of shock, because it is the twelfth of June, and there are only three days left.
Hannay realises that he cannot wait for a letter from Sir Harry any longer. He remembers the village where Sir Harry said that Sir Walter has his country house, and he decides to go there at once.
The fisherman says that his old car is waiting in the lane and that he will gladly drive Hannay to the station. Hannay accepts with real gratitude, but he tries not to show his face to anyone.
At the station the fisherman guesses that Hannay has no money. Without a single question he lends him a few pounds, shakes his hand warmly and wishes him good luck on his journey.
Hannay boards a night train that is going south and wedges himself into the corner of an empty carriage. He sleeps heavily and dreams of Scudder, and the wheels beat out the same words over and over.
Hannay leaves the train at a small station in the south of England and walks through the quiet lanes towards the village. The fields are green and peaceful, and nobody pays any attention to him.
At night Hannay reaches Sir Walter Bullivant's house, a grand country home at the end of a long gravel drive. He climbs the steps, stands before the tall door and knocks.
A stiff butler opens the door and looks coldly at the muddy stranger on the step. Hannay says that he must see Sir Walter at once, because he brings an urgent message from a man called Scudder.
The butler leads Hannay across a hall hung with portraits and into a quiet study lit by a green lamp. A grey-haired, tired-looking man rises from behind the desk, and this is Sir Walter Bullivant.
Hannay gives his name, and he adds that he knows the police are looking for him. He says that he did not kill Scudder, and Sir Walter nods and quietly asks him to sit down.
Hannay tells the whole story from the first knock at his door to the long flight across the moor. Sir Walter listens without a word, only making a few short notes on a sheet of paper.
