Hannay unbuttons his shirt, unties the string and lays the small black notebook on the desk. Sir Walter picks it up carefully, like a man handling a priceless thing that might break.

Sir Walter says quietly that Scudder worked for him, and that he was one of his best men. He had feared the worst when the reports stopped, and for a long time after Hannay's story he sits without speaking.
At last Sir Walter looks up and tells Hannay that he believes every word. Scudder's last reports had been hinting at the same thing for months, and Hannay's story fits them like a key in a lock.

Sir Walter explains that Karolides will be guarded, and that the real danger is of another kind. The spies want the secret plans that the French general and the British leaders will draw up on 15 June.
Sir Walter promises that Hannay is safe in his house, and he rings for hot water, food and clean clothes. For the first time in nearly three weeks, Hannay sits down to a real meal at a real table.
Hannay falls into a real bed and sleeps at once, deeply and without dreams. Down in the study Sir Walter locks the notebook in his safe and sits up late, reading the pages that Hannay has decoded.
In the morning Sir Walter tells Hannay that he has already sent word to London. The French general will arrive tomorrow, and every man who needs to know has been warned to be careful.
A telegram arrives to say that Karolides has reached London safely and is under guard. Sir Walter tells Hannay that he must stay hidden in the house, for the police are still looking for him.
That afternoon Sir Walter and Hannay read the notebook together and try to guess the meaning of the thirty-nine steps. Sir Walter thinks that it could be a pier, a harbour stair or a cliff path.
In the evening Sir Walter leaves for London to make sure that the meeting is properly guarded. He tells Hannay to rest and wait, and to read any book in the library that he likes.
Hannay cannot read or sleep, and all through the next morning he walks restlessly round the garden. He turns the clues over in his mind, but he cannot make them fit together.

In London on the fifteenth, a French general in a plain suit shakes hands with the British leaders. The secret meeting is held behind closed doors, and it ends quietly, with nothing apparently going wrong.

Sir Walter returns late in the afternoon and says that the meeting passed without any trouble. Hannay should be glad, but he is not comforted, and he says that this is exactly what the spies would want.
Hannay says that if the spies have already copied the plans, they will leave England tonight. The notebook says high tide at seventeen minutes past ten, and it is nearly five o'clock already.

Sir Walter pulls heavy books from the library shelves, and the two men search through them for tide tables. At last Sir Walter finds a thick book with the times of the tides all round the English coast.
Hannay runs his finger down the column for the fifteenth of June. At one place on the coast of Kent, a little town called Bradgate, high water is exactly at seventeen minutes past ten.
Sir Walter remembers an old friend who lives a mile away, a retired naval officer who knows the coast of Kent very well. He sends a car to fetch him at once, and the waiting seems endless.
The old naval officer arrives in a few minutes, a brisk, white-whiskered man with a stout stick. He listens eagerly while Sir Walter explains, and then he says that he knows Bradgate very well.
The old officer says that Bradgate is a small place with a handful of villas on a high chalk cliff. One of them, a white house called Trafalgar Lodge, has a private stair that goes down to the beach.
When he hears the word stair, Hannay leaps to his feet. He is certain that the thirty-nine steps lead down the cliff at Trafalgar Lodge, and that the boat will wait at the bottom.
Sir Walter picks up the telephone and calls Scotland Yard. He asks for a trusted detective called Inspector Scaife and tells him to come at once with a few good men and say nothing.
Inspector Scaife arrives within the hour, a broad, quiet man with shrewd eyes. He looks hard at Hannay, who is the man he has been hunting, and then, to everyone's surprise, he holds out his hand.
Scaife listens to the whole story with folded arms. He says that it explains many puzzling things, such as the milkman's story about a gold coin and a joke on some friends.
Scaife says that if they arrest the spies too early, they will lose the plans for ever. They must catch them in the act, and so he sets off with six men in plain clothes in two cars.
The cars race along the narrow lanes of Kent as the sun sets in a red blaze. Sir Walter watches the clock on the dashboard and urges the driver to go faster, for there is very little time left.
As the last light fades they reach Bradgate, and the cars stop on a quiet road out of sight. Ahead of them, on a high cliff above the grey sea, Hannay sees a white house with lighted windows.
Scaife places his men quietly along the lanes and tells them to show no lights. Then he leads Hannay along a high hedge towards the garden of Trafalgar Lodge, moving on tiptoe in the dusk.
Through the gap in the hedge they see three men in white flannels playing tennis on a smooth lawn. They laugh and call out the score, and they look as harmless as three holidaymakers.

Scaife whispers that the three players look like perfectly ordinary gentlemen, and he asks Hannay whether he is quite sure. Hannay can only say that he cannot tell yet, because the light is bad and their faces are turned away.
A ball flies high over the net and into the hedge. One of the players strolls over to fetch it, so close to the hiding place that Hannay could reach out and touch his sleeve.
As the player straightens up with the ball in his hand, his eyelids slide slowly across his eyes like a hawk's. Hannay's heart leaps, because he knows him at once as the bald old man from the moor.
Hannay whispers into Scaife's ear that this is the leader of the Black Stone. Scaife nods, but he says that they must wait for the boat, because the plans are not yet in the water.
Scaife sends his men softly to the garden gates and the sides of the house. Hannay slips away round the edge of the garden, because he wants to find the cliff stair and see it with his own eyes.
At the edge of the garden, where the lawn ends in a low fence, Hannay finds a gate and a long wooden stair. It goes straight down the face of the cliff to the beach, and he begins to climb down.
Counting under his breath, Hannay goes down the steep stair one step at a time. He reaches the bottom, and he can hardly believe it, because there are exactly thirty-nine steps.
From the beach Hannay looks out across the bay. A white yacht lies at anchor near the shore, and he can just read the name Ariadne on her bow.
Hannay climbs back up the thirty-nine steps and creeps to Scaife's side. He whispers that the stair is real, that the yacht is waiting in the bay, and that the tide is already rising.
The three men finish their game and go into the house, and the lamps in the windows glow brightly. A little before ten they come out again in dark coats, and one of them carries a small leather case.
The wind drops, and the sound of the waves on the shingle grows louder as the tide rises. In the shadows of the hedge, Scaife's men crouch in the dark and wait, hardly daring to cough.
Far below, a tiny light moves slowly across the dark water towards the beach. Hannay leans over the cliff and hears the soft creak of oars, and he knows that the yacht's boat is coming in.
The three men walk swiftly across the lawn towards the cliff stair. They pass so close to the hidden policemen that Hannay can hear the old man's quiet breathing and smell his tobacco.
As the three men reach the gate of the stair, Scaife blows his whistle. The policemen spring out of the shadows on every side, and in a moment the three men are surrounded.
The two younger men struggle and shout, but the old man stands stiff and silent between two officers. In the confusion the leather case falls on the grass, and Scaife stoops quickly to pick it up.
Scaife tells the three men that they are under arrest. The old man says quietly that he is no archaeologist at all but a faithful servant of his own country, which is Germany.
Down on the beach, the yacht's boat grounds on the shingle. Policemen and coastguards, who have been waiting in the dark, seize the sailors before they can row away.
Out in the bay a naval patrol boat switches on a searchlight and holds the Ariadne in its bright beam. The yacht's captain sees that he is caught, and he does not try to run away.
While the prisoners are led away, Scaife and Sir Walter search the white house. In a quiet study on the ground floor they find a large desk, and on it a neat pile of papers under a lamp.

In the leather case and in the desk drawers, Sir Walter finds the copied plans of the secret meeting. He checks every sheet with the greatest care, and a deep look of relief spreads over his tired face.
In the drawers they also find the papers of the Black Stone itself, with lists of names, codes and addresses. Scaife whistles softly, because the plot reached across the whole of Britain.
On the dark lawn Sir Walter takes Hannay's hand in both of his. He says quietly that Scudder would have been proud, and that Hannay has finished the work that Scudder began.
Scotland Yard announces that Hannay's name is cleared, and he is free to walk the London streets again. He hunts for the cheerful milkman who lent him his coat, and he gives him another gold coin.

Sir Walter arranges that Scudder shall be buried with honour in a quiet churchyard. Hannay stands beside the grave with a few grave-faced men from the Foreign Office, and he thinks of the thin man with bright eyes.
On the twenty-eighth of June the heir to the Austrian throne is shot in Sarajevo. The great powers begin to quarrel, and day by day Europe slides further towards the war that Scudder had feared.
On the fourth of August Britain declares war on Germany. Crowds fill the London streets, and the newspaper boys shout the headlines, and Hannay knows that the great war has begun at last.
Hannay goes at once to join the army, and he is accepted gladly. The dull, empty feeling that sent him for his ship in May has gone for ever, because now he has a purpose.

Before he leaves for training, Hannay stands once more at the top of the cliff stair at Bradgate and looks out over the sea. He thinks of the stranger whose knock at his door began the whole adventure.
C1C2: In the spring of 1914, Richard Hannay, a mining engineer who had spent long hard years under the hot sun of Rhodesia, stepped off a ship and into the grey drizzle of a London afternoon. He had made money enough to live as he pleased, and for years he had pictured this city as the centre of the world, full of old friends, good talk and endless amusement. It had never occurred to him that a man might arrive with a full pocket and an empty heart.

During his first weeks in London, Hannay bought a wardrobe of respectable clothes, strolled through the great streets and stood before every famous building that the guidebooks recommended. The pleasure of it faded far more quickly than he had expected, like a bright coin that turns out to be copper. By the end of the month he had seen everything worth seeing and felt nothing at all.

Friends of friends invited him to clubs and dining tables where well-dressed men discussed horses, golf, house prices and the failings of their servants with an earnestness that astonished him. He listened politely and answered when he was spoken to, yet every conversation seemed to take place behind a pane of glass. A man who had faced fever and danger on the open veldt found that he could hardly stifle a yawn over the soup.

The newspapers that spring were full of quarrels among the great powers of Europe, and above all of unrest in the Balkans, where one small state seemed always to be threatening another. Hannay, who had been out of the world for years, listened with half an ear while the members of his club assured one another that nothing serious could come of it. The whole continent, they said, was far too rich and too sensible to go to war.

He walked for hours through the crowded streets, watching the pale, hurried faces that streamed past him as though each one were late for an appointment that mattered. Somewhere under that low grey sky, he thought, there must be a purpose behind all this bustle, but he could not find it. His mind kept returning to the wide, burning heaven of Rhodesia, where a man could see for fifty miles and nobody asked him anything.

At last, late one evening in May, Hannay made up his mind with the calm of a man who has been defeated by boredom. If nothing happened to change his life before the month was out, he would book a passage on the first ship sailing south and go home to the sun. He felt better at once, as a prisoner might who has finally counted the days to his release.

He dined alone at his club that evening, and afterwards, instead of taking a cab, he walked home through streets that were slowly turning from gold to violet. The long May dusk lay over London like a gentle hand, and for a moment the great city seemed almost kind. A few early lamps were lit, and somewhere a barrel organ was playing an old tune that he half remembered.

In his flat in Portland Place he threw open the window, lit his pipe and let the sounds of the street drift up to him, the clatter of hooves, the hooting of motor horns and the murmur of voices below. None of it touched him, for his thoughts had flown far away to Africa. He was remembering a camp fire on the veldt, the smell of wood smoke and the huge, patient silence of the stars.

He took down a printed list of sailings and ran a finger along the column of dates, as a man might who is choosing the day of his own rescue. In the morning, he resolved, he would call at the shipping office, pay for a cabin and be done with the whole dull business of London. The thought pleased him so much that he laughed aloud in the empty room.

He had just reached the end of his pipe when a quick, nervous knock sounded at the door. Hannay opened it and found on the landing a thin, sandy-moustached man with a brown face and bright, restless eyes, whom he knew by sight as a neighbour from the same building. The visitor's hands were trembling, and he kept glancing over his shoulder at the empty stairs.

The visitor gave his name as Scudder and asked, in a low voice, whether he might come in for a few minutes. No sooner was he inside than he shot the bolt on the door, hurried to the window and drew back the edge of the curtain just far enough to study the street below. Hannay watched him with growing curiosity, for the man moved like a hunted animal.

Without being asked to sit, Scudder begged for a glass of whisky, and he swallowed it in two quick gulps while his hand shook so much that the glass rang against his teeth. Yet his eyes were sharp and clear, and there was nothing of the drunkard or the lunatic in them. Hannay, who had seen men go white with fear in the mining camps, recognised the look at once.

Leaning forward in the armchair, Scudder asked whether Hannay was a man who could keep a secret and keep it well. He had been observing his neighbour for some days, he admitted, and had decided that a man so newly arrived from abroad, with no ties in London and no taste for gossip, was exactly the person he needed. Hannay, who had been bored for weeks, was not sure whether to feel flattered or merely alarmed.

In a whisper that made the hair stand up on the back of Hannay's neck, Scudder declared that he would be a dead man within a few days unless someone gave him shelter. Hannay, who was a practical person, suggested that the police were the proper people to ask. The little man gave a bitter laugh and replied that the police would listen politely, write nothing down and send him away.

Scudder explained that he was an American who had wandered through the capitals of Europe for many years, though not as a tourist and not exactly as a newspaper man. He had sat in cafes, hotel lounges and railway waiting rooms, listening to men who believed that no one was paying them any attention. A good deal of what he had learned, he said, had already gone to people who mattered.

People imagined that a great war came by accident, like a thunderstorm, said Scudder, but that was not the whole truth. In the darkness behind the newspapers and the speeches, a small number of patient men had decided that Europe must burn, and they were arranging the matches with all the care of a watchmaker. Hannay smiled politely, though the little man's solemn earnestness was beginning to trouble him more than he cared to admit.

The first of the matches, Scudder went on, was a Greek statesman named Karolides, the prime minister of his country, who was due to arrive in London on the fifteenth of June. He was an honest and respected man who had worked for years to keep the peace between his neighbours, and for that reason he had to be removed. Scudder gave the date and the place, and he said them as flatly as a clerk reading out a railway timetable.

A murder in the heart of London, with the world watching, would be a spark in a barn full of dry straw, Scudder insisted. The great nations of Europe had bound themselves by treaties and secret promises, and every army was ready, so that one violent act would drag the whole continent into the fire. In the confusion, nobody would stop to ask who had really planned it, or why.

To Hannay's ear the whole business sounded like the sort of wild tale that a man might invent over a long dinner, and he said as much, though kindly. Scudder only shook his head wearily, like a doctor who has met a hundred sceptical patients. There was something so honest in the little man's fear that Hannay found it impossible to laugh.

Reaching into his coat, Scudder drew out a small black notebook with a worn cover and held it up between two fingers as though it were made of glass. Its pages were crowded with columns of figures and curious signs that meant nothing to Hannay, but Scudder tapped it and said that the whole truth was written inside. If those pages were ever lost, he added quietly, a great many people would die for it.

The conspirators, Scudder said, had a name for themselves, and the name was the Black Stone. They were patient and clever and quite without pity, and they had already removed more than one inconvenient person who had come too close to their secret. He pronounced the words in a whisper, as though the walls of the flat might repeat them.

Their leader, Scudder said, was an old man, calm, courteous and soft of voice, whom a stranger might easily take for a retired schoolmaster. The one feature that betrayed him was his eyelids, which could slide across his eyes from the side, exactly as a hawk's do when it watches its prey. Scudder swore that anyone who had once seen that slow, chilling gesture would never be able to forget it.

He had learned too much, Scudder confessed, and had been careless enough to let them find out. A fortnight earlier he had been caught listening in a place where no stranger was supposed to be, and he had escaped only because the door was left open and the night was dark. Since then he had lived like a rabbit with dogs in the next field.

Three times in two weeks he had changed his lodgings, said Scudder, and three times he had believed himself safe. That very afternoon, however, he had noticed a man loitering at the corner of this street who looked unpleasantly like one he had seen in another city, and he did not think it was a coincidence. The stranger, he was certain, had been watching the door of the building and not the passing traffic.

For a long moment Hannay studied the thin, brown, frightened face across the table. He thought of the dull weeks behind him and the ship that was waiting to carry him home, and it struck him that true or false, this was the first thing in London that had stirred his blood. Slowly he nodded, and he told Scudder, in a voice that surprised even himself, that he would help him.

Hannay offered the little spare room at the back of the flat, which had a narrow bed, a table and a window that looked on to a blank wall. Scudder thanked him with a warmth that was almost painful, and then he made one condition: that Hannay should tell no living soul, not even his oldest friend, that he was there. Hannay gave his word without a moment's hesitation, and he meant every syllable of it.

Before he went to bed, Scudder asked for paper, a bottle of ink and a supply of pens, and he carried them with the black notebook into the spare room. He said that he had a great deal to put in order before it was too late, and that he would be working into the small hours. The door closed softly behind him, and Hannay was left alone with the silence.

Hannay lay awake for a long while, listening to the steady scratching of the pen on the other side of the wall, which went on and on like the sound of a patient mouse. Now and then footsteps passed along the street below, slowed outside the building and went on, and each time he found himself holding his breath. It was a long time since a night had held so much interest for him.

In the morning light Scudder seemed a different man, calmer and steadier, and he ate a large breakfast with every sign of enjoyment. He told Hannay that he knew a certain man in high office who could stop the whole conspiracy if only he could be convinced, and that he meant to reach him before the middle of June. Until the moment was right, he said, it was safest to stay out of sight.

Towards evening Hannay put on his coat and announced that he would dine out, for even a man with a secret cannot live on bread and anxiety for ever. At the door Scudder pressed the black notebook into his hand and begged him to keep it in his pocket, since it would be safe nowhere else. It was, as events would prove, the last time that Hannay ever saw him alive.

It was long after midnight when Hannay climbed the stairs, pleasantly tired after a good dinner and an hour at a music hall. He slid his key into the lock and went in, but the flat was dark and strangely silent, and the quiet had a heavy quality that made him stop in the hall. When at last he called out Scudder's name, nobody answered, and the silence seemed to listen.

Hannay struck a match, lit the lamp and then stood quite still in the doorway of the sitting room. Scudder lay on his back upon the carpet with his arms flung wide, and a long knife had been driven through his heart and into the floor beneath him. There was no need to feel for a pulse, for the little man's bright eyes were fixed on the ceiling and he had plainly been dead for some time.

For some minutes after he had seen it, Hannay could neither move nor think. The clock on the mantelpiece went on ticking with a calm and even beat, as though nothing in the world had changed, and that ordinary sound seemed to him more horrible than any scream. Only gradually did he begin to understand that the man who had been alive and joking at breakfast was now a lifeless stranger.

A walk through the flat showed him that the killers had been thorough, for every drawer was pulled open, the cushions had been slit and the contents of the spare room were strewn across the floor. They had been looking for something, and with a cold shock Hannay understood what it was. The black notebook was sitting in the inner pocket of his own coat, where Scudder had begged him to keep it.

Slowly, as he sat in the lamplight, the danger took shape in his mind, and it was not a pleasant shape. A man lay murdered in his flat, no one else knew that the victim had been there, and the only story Hannay could tell was about secret societies, Greek statesmen and hawk-eyed old men. If he were the police, he thought, he would arrest such a man without a moment's hesitation, for it all sounded like the ravings of a lunatic.

Crouching beside the window, Hannay drew back the edge of the curtain and looked down into the street. Two men were standing there in the pale light of the lamps, one in the shadow of a doorway and one at the corner, and neither of them was looking at anything but the entrance to his building. They were not policemen, he felt sure, for they stood with a patience that no policeman ever showed.

Spreading a map and a railway guide before him on the table, Hannay considered where a hunted man might hide himself. London was impossible and the south of England too crowded and too well policed, but the north held huge tracts of empty country where a stranger could walk for days without meeting anyone. His eye fell on Galloway in the south-west of Scotland, a wide country of hills and moor, and his heart gave a small leap.

Towards five o'clock, when the windows had begun to grey, Hannay heard the clink of cans on the stairs and a cheerful whistle drawing nearer. It was the milkman, a regular and faithful visitor who came at the same hour every morning and who, as far as Hannay could tell, had never once been suspected of anything. An idea came to him with such sudden force that he almost laughed aloud in the grey silence.

Opening the door a crack, Hannay beckoned the milkman in and told him a story about a wager and a few friends waiting in the street below who needed to be fooled. He offered a gold coin for the loan of the man's white coat, his cap and his round of cans, and he promised to leave them in a safe place. The man stared at the coin for a long moment, scratched his head and then burst out laughing.

Within five minutes Hannay stood in the hall in the milkman's cap and coat with the brim pulled low over his eyes and a pair of heavy cans swinging in his hands. He looked in the mirror and saw a stranger, an honest, sleepy, unremarkable working man, and he drew a long breath. Then, with a heart that was thumping like a drum, he pushed open the street door and walked out into the morning.

Hannay walked down the middle of the pavement with his cans swinging, whistling a tuneless little song through his teeth. His path took him within a few paces of the man in the doorway and then of the man at the corner, and he felt their eyes pass over him like a cold draught. His heart was beating so loudly that he was certain they must hear it.

One of the two men turned his head and looked straight at him, and for the space of a heartbeat Hannay's blood ran cold. Then the stranger's gaze slid off the white coat and the heavy cans as it might slide off a lamp post, and he turned back to watch the door of the building. No one pays any attention to a milkman, Hannay thought, and he blessed the dull faces of the world.

Round the first corner, in a quiet side street where no one was stirring, Hannay pulled off the white coat and the cap and folded them neatly beside the cans on a doorstep. The honest milkman would find them there when he came looking, and he would be richer by a gold coin and a very good story. Hannay straightened his jacket, drew a deep breath and set off at a brisk walk.

The great railway station was already filling with early travellers, porters and newsboys, and Hannay stood for a time before the long board of departures, as though he were choosing a holiday. Then he made his choice and bought a third-class ticket for a small station in Galloway, a place so remote that no sensible hunter would ever look for him there. The clerk behind the little window did not even raise his eyes as he stamped the ticket.

With a long whistle the train drew out of the station, and the roofs and chimneys of London slid slowly past the window like a dull and sooty dream. Hannay wedged himself into the corner of a third-class carriage with his cap over his eyes and breathed freely for the first time since midnight. Behind him lay a murdered man, a watching street and an empty flat, and in his pocket lay a small black notebook.

Hour after hour the green fields rolled past the window, and the wheels beat out their steady rhythm beneath the floor. Hannay thought of Scudder, of his bright, frightened eyes and his cheerful wave from the sitting room door, and he felt that he owed the little man a debt. That debt could only be paid by finishing what Scudder had begun, and he resolved to stay free until the fifteenth of June, whatever it cost.

At a large station on the way north he bought an evening newspaper from a boy on the platform and opened it with a hand that was not quite steady. A short paragraph reported a murder in Portland Place, and it added that the police were anxious to speak to the tenant of the flat, one Richard Hannay, who had recently come from Africa. Seeing his own name in print gave him an odd, unpleasant feeling, as though he were reading about a stranger.

A stout and talkative passenger in a tweed coat had read the same paragraph, and he announced to the whole carriage that the wretched murderer would certainly be caught before the week was out. Hannay raised his newspaper until it hid his face and murmured that he hoped so too. It struck him that there is no company in the world so entertaining as that of a man who is talking about you without knowing it.

As the light faded, Hannay changed at a junction to a slow, small train that wandered along a branch line into emptier and wilder country. The fields gave way to stone walls and long brown slopes, the stations grew smaller and the lamps on the platforms fewer, and one by one the other passengers climbed out and vanished into the dusk. By the time the train reached the last stretch of its journey, he had the whole carriage to himself.

At last the little train wheezed to a stop at a station that consisted of one wooden platform, one lamp and one sleepy porter, and Hannay stepped down into the cool dark. The air was sharp and clean and smelled of heather and peat smoke, and after the stale warmth of the carriage it seemed to him the sweetest thing he had ever breathed. Without a glance at the porter, he turned and walked quickly away into the night.

He left the station behind and followed a rough lane until the last lamp had vanished, and then he climbed a long slope onto the open moor under a sky that was crowded with stars. In the lee of an old stone wall he found a hollow thick with heather, and he lay down in it with his coat pulled tight around him. Cold, hungry and hunted as he was, he fell asleep almost at once, and nothing disturbed him until morning.

He woke at daybreak to the wild, bubbling song of the larks, stiff in every limb and wet with dew, and he sat up to look at the world. Brown hills rolled away in every direction beneath the pale sky, small lochs glinted like silver coins in the hollows, and there was not a roof or a chimney to be seen. For the first time in many weeks, he felt something very close to simple happiness.

Sitting on a flat stone, Hannay emptied his pockets and took stock of his fortune, which amounted to a little silver, a few ship's biscuits and the black notebook. The arithmetic was not encouraging, but the plan was clear enough in his mind. He must keep away from towns and railway stations, buy food where he could and stay out of sight for about three weeks, until the fifteenth of June had come and gone.

Late that morning he met an old shepherd with two black-and-white dogs at his heels, who looked him up and down with the calm curiosity of a man who sees few strangers. Hannay explained that he was a visitor on a walking holiday and that he was looking for a bed and a meal, and the old man, after a long pause, pointed with his stick to the east. There was an inn, he said, a few hours' walk away, kept by a decent man who asked no questions.

Not wishing to arrive at the inn in broad daylight, Hannay wandered on and presently came upon an empty stone cottage beside a stream, with a table, a bench and a roof that was nearly whole. It was a place where a shepherd had once sheltered in the lambing season and which no one had visited for a long time. Hannay washed his face in the cold water, ate a biscuit and decided to stay there until nightfall.

When darkness fell, Hannay lit a stub of candle that he had found on a shelf and opened the black notebook for the first time since leaving London. Page after page was covered with neat columns of figures in Scudder's small, upright hand, and the flame shook slightly in the draught as he turned the leaves. It was clear that the notebook held a secret, and equally clear that he would need all his wits to open it.

Here and there among the endless columns, Scudder had written a few words in plain English, as a man might leave a few lighted windows in a dark street. Hannay found a handful of names, some dates, a mention of Karolides and, near the end, two puzzling words, thirty-nine steps. They meant nothing to him at that moment, but Scudder had underlined them twice, as a man does with what he fears to forget.

In his years among the mines Hannay had met a few simple codes, and he guessed that the numbers stood for letters according to some key, probably a word or a name known only to Scudder. He tried every word that he could remember from the notebook, and then every word that Scudder had spoken in the flat, working through the night on a scrap of paper. Each attempt, however carefully he worked it through, produced nothing but a jumble of meaningless letters.

As the window turned from black to grey, Hannay tried one last name that Scudder had mentioned in the flat, and he caught his breath, because the first line of figures changed under his pencil into letters. He worked on feverishly, with the candle guttering beside him and his tiredness forgotten, and the letters ran into words and the words into sentences. He was holding, in his own two hands, the voice of the dead man who had trusted him.

The first decoded sentences made him stare as if the paper had spoken aloud. Scudder had written that the planned murder of Karolides, which he had described so earnestly in the flat, was only a trick, a bright decoy to draw every eye. Behind it, he said, lay something far larger and far more dangerous, and Hannay sat motionless with the pencil in his hand and read on.

Scudder's notes were brisk and orderly, like the report of a careful clerk, and they stated at the outset that the Black Stone worked for Germany. Its members were spies, patient, educated and well supplied with money, whose real business was to discover British secrets and carry them safely across the sea. The murders and the whispered threats, it appeared, were merely the tools of their trade.

The murder of Karolides, the notes explained, had never been the real purpose of the plot but only a piece of theatre. While the newspapers shouted about Greece and the Balkans and the statesmen wrung their hands, nobody would think to look at what the Black Stone was really doing in a quiet room in London. It was the oldest trick of the conjuror, to make the audience stare at the wrong hand.

On that same fifteenth of June, according to Scudder, a French general named Royer was to visit London in strict secrecy and meet certain British leaders in a private room. They would settle how the navies of the two countries should work together if war ever came, and every detail of the arrangement would be written down. Such a paper would be worth more to an enemy than a hundred battleships.

The Black Stone, Scudder had discovered, knew the date and the place of the meeting, and it had made its arrangements with chilling thoroughness. As soon as the talks were over, its agents would copy the plans, and no one would suspect that anything was missing until the damage was done. Reading this by the failing light of the candle, Hannay understood at last why Scudder had been so frightened.

The plans, Scudder believed, would be carried out of the country by sea, since the spies dared not trust them to the post or the railway, and the boat would leave at night on the top of the tide. He had written down only two clues, the words thirty-nine steps and the hour, seventeen minutes past ten, and beside them a question mark. Evidently he had not yet discovered where the boat was to wait, nor the name of the place.

Thirty-nine steps, Hannay mused, might belong to a church tower, a lighthouse, the stairs of a London hotel or any one of ten thousand other places, and he could make nothing of it. Yet the number was so exact, and Scudder had underlined it so firmly, that it must be a clue of the greatest importance. He turned the puzzle over and over in his mind, from every possible angle, until his head began to ache.

At the foot of the last decoded page Scudder had added a short note in his tidy hand, and the note held a name. If anything should happen to him, it said, the notebook must reach Bullivant at the Foreign Office, who alone would know how to use it and who alone could be trusted to believe it. Now, at last, Hannay understood what Scudder had meant when he spoke so hopefully of a man in high office.

It was one thing to know the name of the man he must see and quite another to reach him. A fugitive wanted for murder could not simply stroll into the Foreign Office, give his name at the door and ask for an interview, and Hannay did not even know where Bullivant lived. He needed time, a safe place and above all someone respectable who would take his word.

Taking a length of string from his pocket, Hannay tied the black notebook flat against his chest, under his shirt, where no pickpocket could reach it and no casual search would find it. He fed his rough working papers to the candle flame, one sheet at a time, and he kept the key to Scudder's cipher where no one could ever steal it, inside his own head. Then, with the notebook secure against his heart, he pinched out the candle and sat for a while in the darkness.

He slept for a few hours, ate the last of the biscuits and spent the rest of the day wandering across the moor, keeping to the high ground and avoiding every road and track. Towards dusk, when his legs were aching and the hills had turned the colour of plums, he saw a small yellow light shining in a distant valley. It could only be the inn that the shepherd had described, and Hannay quickened his pace.

The inn was a long, low building of grey stone, with a single lit window, a painted sign that creaked in the evening wind and a thin thread of smoke leaning from its chimney. Hannay knocked at the heavy door and stood waiting on the step, tired to the bone, while slow footsteps came across a stone floor towards him. He had not felt so grateful for a closed door opening in all his life.

The innkeeper proved to be a tall, stooping man with a long grey moustache, a thoughtful forehead and extraordinarily kind eyes. He held up his lamp and looked for a moment at the dusty, unshaven stranger on his step, and then he stood aside and bade him enter without asking a single question. Hannay decided on the spot that he liked this gentle, grey-moustached man very much indeed, and he was glad to have found him.

In the warm kitchen, beside a fire of glowing peat, the innkeeper set before his guest a supper of eggs, bacon, oatcakes and a huge pot of strong tea. Hannay ate with the unashamed appetite of a man who has lived for two days on biscuits, and the innkeeper watched him with quiet pleasure. When the plates were empty, Hannay paid for his room and his meal in advance.

Every wall of the little parlour beyond the kitchen was lined with shelves of battered, much-loved books, and the innkeeper explained with shy pride that he had read every adventure he could lay hands on. In a lonely place like this, he said, a man's only travelling was done in print, and there was nothing he enjoyed so much as a good story. He looked hopefully at his guest, as a dog looks at a closed door.

Feeling that he owed his host something in return for such kindness, Hannay told a tale from his years in Africa, of a river crossing at night, a swollen torrent and a camp in the middle of a storm. He left out everything that might betray his purpose, and the innkeeper listened with shining eyes, his pipe forgotten and his mouth a little open. When it was over, the old man sighed like a boy at the end of a holiday.

On a chair beside the fire lay a London newspaper two days old, folded back to a column that Hannay could read upside down. In thick black letters it announced the mystery of the murder in Portland Place, and under the headline he could make out the words police and flat and missing tenant. He kept his face quite still, and he felt the string on his chest tighten like a snake.

Following Hannay's glance, the innkeeper picked up the newspaper and confessed that he followed murder cases with the same relish that other men gave to horse races. The police, he declared, were hopeless fellows who could not find their own hats, and a clever fugitive would escape them for ever. Hannay agreed in the most casual voice he could manage, and he had the uncomfortable feeling that his host's gentle eyes lingered on him a moment too long.

The innkeeper led the way up a narrow stair to a little room under the roof, where a narrow bed was made up with clean white sheets and a small window looked out over the road. Hannay lay down in his clothes with the notebook still tied against his chest, and the soft darkness folded over him. For the first time in many long days he slept as soundly and as peacefully as a tired child.

Some hours later he woke with a start and lay listening, not certain what had roused him. A motor car was labouring up the road, its headlamps swept across the ceiling in a long pale arc, and then the engine coughed and fell silent right outside the inn. In that remote valley, at that hour of the night, no visitor could have good news for him.

Hannay crept in his stockinged feet to the head of the stairs and listened to the voices that rose from the kitchen below. Two strangers, one of them speaking with a faint foreign accent, were asking the innkeeper whether a tall, brown-faced man with grey eyes had come that way, and their politeness was thin as ice. The innkeeper answered, very slowly and in his gentlest voice, that he had seen no one of the kind.

Hannay eased the little window open without a sound, swung one leg over the sill and lowered himself onto the sloping roof of a shed. Before he went, he reached back and left a silver coin on the sill for the kind old innkeeper, who deserved far better than to be mixed up in such a business. A moment later he dropped lightly into the dark yard and slipped away behind the stable.

He ran across the fields away from the inn and threw himself flat in a wet ditch beside the road, with his heart thudding against the notebook. Presently the car came crawling by with its lamps turned full on the hedges, and he saw the faces of two men peering out into the darkness, one of them clutching a torch. It was a long time after the sound of the engine had faded before he dared to lift his head.

By the time the dawn came grey and cold over the hills, Hannay was soaked to the knees, plastered with mud and so hungry that his stomach seemed to be eating itself. A road led down the hillside towards a scatter of roofs in the valley, and he followed it with the sinking suspicion that he looked exactly like a man who had spent the night in a ditch. There was nothing to be done about that, he decided, except to straighten his back and walk on boldly.

In the village he bought a loaf, some cheese and a bottle of milk from a small shop, paying with the cheerful air of an honest tramp. On a wall beside the door a poster announced a political meeting in the village hall that very evening, with a distinguished speaker coming from London to address the voters. Hannay thought nothing of it at the time, but the memory of that poster was soon to prove most useful.

In a quiet field behind a thick hedge he ate his bread and cheese with the keenest enjoyment, and then he slept through the whole warm afternoon with his coat over his face. When he woke the sun was low and the air smelled of cut grass, and his strength had returned. He decided to walk on into the dusk, along a road that he knew led through the village.

Just beyond the village a small motor car pulled up beside him with a squeal of brakes, and a young man with an anxious, freckled face leaned out and shouted with relief. Here he was at last, cried the young man, the great man from London, whom they had been waiting for since six o'clock and who must come at once or the whole meeting would collapse. Hannay opened his mouth to correct the mistake, and found that nothing came out.

At that moment, far down the valley road, a pair of headlamps swung round a bend and began to creep slowly towards the village. Hannay recognised the slow, searching speed of the car that had visited the inn, and he knew that the two strangers had not given up. A hall crowded with honest farmers, he reflected, was probably the one place in the whole district where nobody would think of looking for him.

The village hall was packed to the doors with farmers and labourers in their Sunday coats, and the air under the hanging lamps was thick with pipe smoke and expectation. Hannay was hurried up the steps to the platform, where the chairman, a bright-eyed young man named Sir Harry, seized his hand and shook it with the fervour of a drowning man grasping a rope. Hannay realised, with a sinking heart, that he had walked into a political meeting.

While Sir Harry was making his opening remarks, a draught of cold air blew through the hall, and Hannay glanced up to see the two strangers standing in the doorway at the back with their hats in their hands. Their eyes passed slowly over the crowd, face by face, in a way that no mere curiosity could explain. Hannay bent his head as if lost in thought and prayed that the lamps would not be bright enough.

At last Sir Harry finished his remarks, turned to Hannay with a flourish and announced the honoured guest from London, and the hall rose in a roar of welcome. Hannay got slowly to his feet like a man who has stepped off the edge of a cliff and is waiting to see where he will land. The whole room, with its lamps, its smoke and its two secret watchers, waited for him to speak.

Hannay cleared his throat, gripped the edge of the table and began in a voice that was not quite steady. He told the crowd that he knew very little about politics, but a good deal about hard work, wild country and the folly of men who talked while others laboured. A murmur of approval ran through the hall, for the farmers liked a plain speaker.

Warming to his theme, Hannay told them that a nation could drift towards disaster like a sleepwalker moving slowly towards the edge of a cliff. People were so busy with their little quarrels, he said, that they failed to see the great storm gathering beyond the hills. He was surprised to hear himself speak with such conviction, for he was talking of things that he knew to be true.

Remembering a few stories from his years in Africa, Hannay sprinkled the speech with jokes against himself, and the farmers roared with laughter and slapped their knees. The more he rambled, the more the audience seemed to love him, and the cheers rose and rolled round the hall like waves. It struck him that he was making a most extraordinary success of the one thing he had never meant to do.

When at last Hannay sat down, the whole hall rose to its feet in a storm of clapping and stamping, and the lamps shook above his head. Sir Harry leaned across and whispered, with tears of laughter in his eyes, that it was a hundred times better than the speech they had been promised. Hannay muttered something modest, and then he looked towards the back of the hall.

The place where the two strangers had stood was empty, and a few moments later Hannay heard a car start in the street outside and drive away, its engine fading into the night. Perhaps they had decided that no man who spoke so foolishly in public could be the quarry they sought, or perhaps they merely meant to try elsewhere. Either way, he drew a long breath of relief and felt the tightness slowly leave his shoulders at last.

When the last of the farmers had gone home, Sir Harry took Hannay up the hill to his large, comfortable house, talking happily all the way. The real speaker, it seemed, had missed his train and sent no word, and the whole evening would have been ruined if a tall stranger had not walked out of the dusk and saved it. He kept thanking Hannay all the way up the hill, as though he had done something truly heroic and brave.

Late that night, sitting beside the dying fire in Sir Harry's study, Hannay looked long and hard at his host's frank young face and made up his mind. He had no right to deceive a man who had been so generous, and he badly needed a friend, so he told the whole story from the beginning. He described the first knock on his door in Portland Place, the knife, the notebook and the long flight across the moor, and he kept nothing back.

Sir Harry listened from beginning to end without a single question, with his chin on his hand and his eyes on the embers. When Hannay had finished there was a long silence in the room, and then the young man said quietly that he believed every word of it. A man who could make such a speech as Hannay had made, he added, could not possibly be a murderer.

Sir Harry astonished him by announcing that he knew Sir Walter Bullivant very well, because Sir Walter was an old friend of his family and a senior man at the Foreign Office. He would write to him that very night, he said, and he promised to tell nobody a word of Hannay's story, while Hannay must keep out of sight until an answer arrived. It was the first real hope that Hannay had seen since the night he found Scudder lying dead on the carpet.

In the grey morning mist Sir Harry came out into the yard with a bundle of old country clothes, a battered cap and a pair of stout boots, and he pressed them into Hannay's hands. Nobody would know him in those, he said cheerfully, and he gave his word again that no whisper of this adventure would pass his lips. A small motor car stood waiting by the gate with its engine murmuring softly in the stillness of the morning.

Sir Harry drove Hannay for an hour along empty lanes and set him down at a lonely crossroads, where a signpost pointed to nothing in particular. He promised again to write to Sir Walter that very day, and he told Hannay to keep walking south through the hills until he heard from him. They shook hands warmly, and the little car went bumping away until the hedges hid it.

In the borrowed tweed jacket, the baggy trousers and the battered cap, Hannay looked like any farm hand on his way to market, and he found that the disguise gave him a curious sense of freedom. The sun was warm on his shoulders, the hedges were loud with birds and the road ran on ahead of him like a ribbon, and for an hour he almost forgot that he was hunted. It was a morning that seemed to have been made for walking, and for forgetting one's troubles.

At a bend in the road Hannay came upon an old man in round spectacles who sat on a heap of stones, tapping them into small pieces with a hammer. It would have seemed strange to walk by without a word, so he stopped and remarked on the fine weather. The old man replied in a slow, rusty voice that it was no bad day for the time of year, and everything about the scene was as ordinary as bread.

While they talked, the old man's eyes slid down to Hannay's feet and rested there for rather longer than politeness allowed. They were fine boots, he remarked at last in his slow voice, very fine indeed for a man in such old clothes, and he said it without any smile. Hannay felt a small cold finger run down his spine, for Sir Harry's good leather had given him away.

Then the old man began to ask questions, idly, as if only to pass the time, about where Hannay had come from, where he was going and what his business might be. His voice was dull and sleepy, yet behind the thick spectacles his eyes were as sharp and alert as a bird's, and they did not belong to a labourer who broke stones for a living. Hannay answered as vaguely as he could, said that he must be getting on, and walked quickly away.

Hannay walked on up the long hill with his hands in his pockets, and when he had gone a hundred yards he looked back over his shoulder. The old man had stopped his work and stood quite upright in the road with his spectacles in his hand, gazing after him with a keenness that was no longer sleepy at all. For a moment it seemed to Hannay that he had seen that face before.

On the crest of the hill he stopped, because a strange humming had begun in the sky, and he looked up to see a small aeroplane crawling over the moor not far above the hilltops. In that year an aeroplane was still a marvel, and in so remote a district it was an astonishing sight. Hannay stood and stared at it with the open mouth of a boy at a fair.

The aeroplane banked, turned and began to circle slowly above the spot where he stood, and a sudden suspicion made Hannay throw himself flat among the heather. Nobody flew in such neat circles over empty moorland for pleasure, and the machine was dropping lower with every turn, like a hawk that has marked a rabbit. He remembered the old man standing in the road with his spectacles in his hand.

Inch by inch he wriggled through the heather to a small stream and slid under the curtain of bracken that hung over its bank, with the cold water soaking his elbows. The aeroplane passed over him twice at the height of a church spire, so low that he could hear the wires singing and see the white face of the pilot looking down. Neither time did the machine stop, and neither time did the pilot seem to see him.

At last the machine dropped lower still, glided over a ridge and landed with a bump on a flat green stretch of moor about a mile away. From the bracken Hannay saw two figures hurrying across the heather towards it and bending to speak to the pilot, and one of them was an old man without spectacles. The whole business was plainly a trap, Hannay realised, and the roadmender had been the bait that drew him into it.

The men from the aeroplane spread out across the hillside and beat the heather and the bracken with sticks, calling to one another in low voices as they went. Hannay lay as still as a stone in the stream bed with his face pressed into the cold moss, and one of them passed so near that he could have touched his boot. As the shadows grew long, the searchers gave up and trudged back to their machine.

At sunset the engine roared, the aeroplane bumped across the turf and rose heavily into the red sky, and it flew away towards the east until it was only a speck and then nothing at all. Hannay waited until the last drone had died away and the moor had grown silent again before he crawled out of the bracken, wet through and stiff with cold. It was not a night on which any sensible man would choose to be out of doors.

The roads were no longer safe, so Hannay struck out across the open moor, steering by the stars and keeping well away from every track and fence. The ground was rough and boggy, and his boots sank into the black peat at nearly every step, and the cold air bit through the borrowed jacket. Behind him lay the road and the roadmender, and ahead of him lay nothing but darkness.

Somewhere in the small hours he stepped into a hidden bog and sank to his knees in the cold black slime, and for a few terrible moments the moor seemed to be swallowing him alive. By dragging himself out inch by inch on his stomach, he reached firm ground at last, plastered with mud, shaking and so hungry that he could have eaten leather. He lay there for a long time, gasping and shivering, before he found the strength to stand up and walk on.

Towards midnight a yellow light blinked out of the darkness ahead, steady and warm, and Hannay stumbled towards it like a moth. It shone from the window of a large, lonely house, which stood at the end of a rough track behind a low stone wall, with a garden full of dark bushes and no neighbour within miles. He hesitated for a moment at the gate, but his hunger and his weariness decided the question for him.

The door was opened by a plump, bald, rosy old gentleman in a velvet jacket, with a round, benevolent face like a good-natured baby's. He took one look at the muddy, shivering traveller on his step and cried out in genuine distress that the poor fellow must come in at once and have something hot to eat. Hannay, who ought to have been suspicious of everything, felt only an overwhelming gratitude.

The old gentleman led his guest into a warm, untidy study crowded with ancient coins, fragments of pottery, rusty swords and glass cases full of mysterious objects. He explained that his one great passion was the study of the Roman past, and while he talked he brought bread, soup and a glass of good red wine. He fussed over his guest like a mother hen, and Hannay ate and drank and felt the tension drain slowly out of his bones.

Over the soup the old gentleman asked, with the gentlest curiosity, where his guest had come from and how he had come to be wandering about the moor at midnight. Hannay told a careful and cheerful tale about a walking holiday that had gone astray, and he said nothing whatever about London, Scudder or the notebook tied against his chest. The old man nodded sympathetically, but Hannay thought that he listened rather too closely.

Soon afterwards a motor car drew up outside the house, a door slammed, and two more guests came into the study, a tall man with a thin, clever face and a pale young man in a flying coat. The old gentleman greeted them as old friends and introduced Hannay with a charming smile, and the newcomers shook hands politely. It was only when the young man's eyes dropped to Hannay's boots that a chill touched him.

As the old gentleman turned his head to speak to the tall man, the lamplight caught his face, and his eyelids slid slowly across his eyes from the side with a motion exactly like that of a hawk. Scudder's whispered description came back to Hannay word for word, and his blood ran cold in his veins. He had stumbled out of the empty moor straight into the lair of the Black Stone, and the leader himself had given him soup.

Before Hannay could rise from his chair, the tall man and the young man had seized him by the arms, and the old gentleman looked on with his gentle, benevolent smile. He apologised for the inconvenience and said, in the tone of a host regretting a cold dinner, that the matter would be discussed in the morning when everyone was rested. Hannay struggled with all his strength, but two strong men held him fast, and he was powerless against them.

They emptied his pockets on the table and found nothing but a few coins, a clasp knife and a scrap of bread, and the tall man swore softly in a foreign tongue. It never occurred to them in their haste to unbutton the shirt of a man who was supposed to be an innocent wanderer, and the black notebook stayed tied against his chest. The old man remarked pleasantly that there was really no hurry, since the guest could not possibly leave before morning.

He was marched up a flight of stairs and thrust into a small, bare room at the end of a passage, with a shuttered window, a narrow bed and a tall cupboard in one corner. The door slammed behind him, a key turned, and the sound of heavy footsteps began to pace up and down the passage. He sat down on the narrow bed in the darkness and listened to the pounding of his own heart, trying to think.

Lying flat with his ear pressed to the floorboards, Hannay could make out fragments of the talk in the study below, the murmur of the old man's smooth voice and the harsher answers of the tall stranger. They spoke of leaving at first light and of the business of the fifteenth, and, with an icy casualness that froze him, of what was to be done with their guest before they went. Cold as ice, he understood that he had until dawn to save his own life, and not a minute longer.

Groping round the room in the dark, he opened the tall cupboard and ran his hands along the shelves, and his fingers closed on a small wooden box among some old tools. Inside lay several sticks of blasting explosive, a coil of fuse and a handful of detonators, the very things that he had handled a thousand times in the African mines. He almost laughed aloud at such extraordinary luck, for the spies had locked him in a room that held the very means of his escape.

A mining engineer knows blasting powder as a cook knows flour, and Hannay turned a stick over in a shaft of moonlight that fell through a crack in the shutter and weighed the matter carefully. There was enough to break a lock, a door and perhaps a wall, but not enough, if he used it wisely, to bring the house down upon his own head. Slowly, as he sat in the half dark with the cold sticks in his hand, a daring plan took shape in his mind.

Working with the swift, sure hands of long practice, he packed a small charge against the door beside the lock, fitted a detonator and cut a length of fuse that would burn for about half a minute. Then he dragged the narrow bed into a corner, turned it on its side to make a shield and settled himself behind it with the mattress over his head. It was a risky business, as he knew very well, but he had no better choice and very little time.

He waited until the voices in the study had died away, the lamps had gone out and the heavy footsteps in the passage had faded to the far end of the house and stopped. Then he struck a match from a box that he had found on the shelf, touched it to the fuse, which sputtered into sullen red life, and dived behind the bed with his hands over his ears. The seconds crawled by like hours, and every tiny creak of the old house made him fear that the guard was returning.

The explosion came like a clap of thunder in a cellar, shaking the whole house to its foundations, and the door was blown off its hinges in a cloud of smoke, splinters and falling plaster. The bed jumped against Hannay's shoulder, and for a moment the world was nothing but a high singing in his ears. Then, through the haze, he saw a ragged hole where the door had been and the pale square of the passage beyond.

Coughing and half blinded, Hannay leapt through the smoking gap, vaulted over the dazed guard, who sat on the floor with his hands over his ears, and flew down the staircase three steps at a time. Shouts rose from every side and a door banged somewhere, but he found a back door in the kitchen passage, wrenched it open and burst out into the cool, dark garden. Behind him, with a growing clamour of voices and slamming doors, the whole house was waking in wild confusion.

He ran across the dark moor as fast as his legs would carry him, leaping heather and splashing through pools, while behind him a red glow rose against the sky where the explosion had set a curtain alight. The sound of shouting followed him for a long way, thin and angry on the night wind. He did not stop until his lungs were on fire and the glow had shrunk to a speck.

Parched with thirst and dizzy with weariness, Hannay stumbled down into a green glen where a stream chattered over the stones, and he knelt and drank like an animal. A little farther along the bank he came upon a quiet man in a tweed hat, standing up to his knees in a pool and flicking a long rod to and fro with the elegant patience of a lifelong angler. The fisherman looked up from his pool without the slightest surprise, as though ragged strangers came down the glen every morning.

The fisherman took one look at the ragged, muddy figure on the bank, laid down his rod and asked no questions at all. He produced a packet of sandwiches and a flask of hot tea from his basket and pressed them on the stranger with the simple courtesy of a man who has been hungry himself. Hannay thought that nothing in his whole life had ever tasted so good, and they sat side by side on a flat stone in the early sun.

Beside the fishing basket lay a folded newspaper, and as Hannay reached for another sandwich his eye fell on the date at the top of the page. It was the twelfth of June, and with a jolt that nearly made him drop his tea he realised that only three days remained before the fifteenth. In all the wandering and hiding of the past fortnight he had lost count of the days.

There was no time left to hide on the hills and wait for letters, and Hannay saw it plainly. Sir Harry had mentioned in passing the name of the English village where Sir Walter Bullivant kept his country house, and Hannay remembered it now. He resolved to go there at once and place the notebook in the one pair of hands that could use it, and if the spies caught him on the way, then so be it.

The fisherman remarked that his old motor car stood in the lane beyond the hedge, and that he would be delighted to drive his new friend to the station in the nearest town. Hannay accepted with heartfelt gratitude, and as they rattled along the road he sat well down in his seat with his cap pulled over his eyes, so that nobody in the passing carts should see his face. All the way, the fisherman talked cheerfully and at great length about trout, and Hannay was glad to listen.

At the station the fisherman, who was evidently a man of sharper eyes than he pretended, guessed that his passenger had no money, and without a single question he pressed a handful of banknotes into his hand. Hannay protested, and the fisherman waved the protest aside, saying that a man ought to repay a kindness whenever he could and that he looked as though he had a long way to go. Then he wished him luck, climbed back into his rattling little car and drove away down the hill without once looking back.

That night Hannay boarded a train bound for the south and wedged himself into the corner of an empty third-class carriage, where he fell at once into a heavy sleep. He dreamed of Scudder, of a small bright face and a long knife and a flight of stairs that went on for ever, and the wheels beneath him beat out the same two words over and over again. At every station he started awake and listened for the tread of the police.

Late the next afternoon he stepped down at a small and sleepy station in the south of England and set off along a winding lane between high hedges, with the evening sun lying in long golden bars across the fields. After the wild moors of Galloway the gentle, well-kept country seemed almost unreal, and nobody who passed him on the road gave the weary tramp so much as a glance. He kept walking steadily through the gathering dusk, along lane after lane, until at last the village lamps were lit.

Night had fallen when he found the house he sought, a large and stately building at the end of a long gravel drive lined with tall limes, with lamps glowing softly in a row of windows. Hannay climbed the steps and stood for a moment before the tall front door, scarcely daring to hope that his long flight had really ended. Then he took a deep breath, lifted the heavy iron knocker and let it fall three times against the oak.

The door was opened by a tall, stiff butler who surveyed the muddy, unshaven stranger on the step as one might survey a spot on the best tablecloth. Hannay said that he must see Sir Walter at once on a matter of the gravest urgency, and when the butler began to shake his head, he added quietly that he brought a message from a man named Scudder. The effect of the name upon that stiff and disapproving servant was instant, and it was quite remarkable to see.

The butler's face changed at once, and without another word he led Hannay across a great hall hung with portraits and into a quiet, book-lined study lit by a single green-shaded lamp. A grey-haired man with a lean, tired, intelligent face rose from behind the desk, and Hannay knew without being told that this was Sir Walter Bullivant. His eyes were keen and weary, like those of someone who has carried a heavy load for many years.

Hannay gave his name and added bluntly that he knew the police were searching for him in connection with a murder in Portland Place, and that he had not committed it. Sir Walter heard him out without any change of expression, and then he said in a soft, dry voice that he had read the newspapers and supposed that Hannay had better sit down. Without another word he pushed a decanter and a glass across the polished desk towards his visitor, and then he settled back to listen.

For nearly an hour Hannay talked, beginning with the knock on his door in Portland Place and continuing through the milkman's coat, the moors, the cipher, the speech, the roadmender, the aeroplane and the old gentleman with the hawk's eyelids. Sir Walter did not interrupt once, and his pen moved only now and then across a sheet of paper, noting a name or a date. Outside the window the night grew quieter, and the fire sank slowly in the grate while the story went on.

Last of all, Hannay unbuttoned his torn shirt, untied the string from his chest and laid the black notebook on the desk between them. Sir Walter took it up with great care, as though it were made of glass, and turned over a few pages, and for the first time his calm face showed some feeling. He said that it was exactly as Hannay had described it, and that he knew that handwriting well.

Scudder had worked for him, Sir Walter said quietly, and had been one of the best and bravest men he had ever sent abroad, and when the reports ceased to arrive some weeks before he had feared the worst. Now that his fear was confirmed, he sat for a long time with his hand over his eyes and said nothing at all. Hannay, understanding that he was in the presence of a real sorrow, kept silent.

At last Sir Walter lifted his head and said that he believed every word Hannay had spoken. Scudder's last reports had been hinting for months at some great and secret scheme, he explained, and the story that Hannay had brought fitted them as a key fits a lock, and nobody could have invented such a tale. Hannay felt a burden roll from his shoulders that he had carried since the night in Portland Place.

Karolides, Sir Walter explained, would be guarded night and day by the best men in the country, and he was in little danger, but the true peril was of another sort altogether. If the paper that was to be drawn up on the fifteenth fell into German hands, an enemy would know how the British and French fleets meant to fight together, and he could plan to beat them. As he spoke he drew a line across the Channel on the map with one steady, thin finger, and Hannay watched it.

Sir Walter promised that Hannay was safe under his roof, since the house was well guarded and no policeman would cross its threshold without his leave. Then he rang for the butler and ordered hot water, a supper and a change of clothes, and soon Hannay was bathed and shaved and sitting down to a proper meal at a proper table. After three weeks of heather, ditches and cold biscuits, he could hardly believe that it was all real.

Hannay fell into a real bed between clean sheets and was asleep before his head touched the pillow, and he did not dream. Downstairs in the study, Sir Walter locked the notebook in his iron safe and sat up late into the night, reading Hannay's pencilled translation again and again and tapping the arm of his chair. Somewhere in those pages, he felt certain, lay the answer to the riddle of the thirty-nine steps.

In the morning Sir Walter told Hannay, between puffs on a cigarette, that he had been busy since dawn with the telephone and the telegraph. The French general would reach London secretly on the following day, he said, and every man who needed to know the truth had been warned to guard his tongue and his papers. It was clear to Hannay that the grey old official, for all his weariness, had not wasted a single minute.

A telegram arrived during the morning with the news that Karolides had reached London safely and that a ring of watchful detectives already surrounded him. Sir Walter read it twice and then told Hannay firmly that he must remain hidden in the house, since the police were still seeking the Portland Place murderer and an arrest now would ruin everything. Hannay, who had never in his life enjoyed sitting still, accepted the order with a long and heavy sigh.

That afternoon the two men bent over the black notebook, going through Hannay's pencilled translation line by line, and returned again and again to the puzzling phrase thirty-nine steps. Sir Walter suggested a harbour stair, a pier, a cliff path or the staircase of some tall house by the water, but none of these guesses led anywhere. It was like trying to open a door when one has the key to the wrong house.

Towards evening Sir Walter drove off to London in his motor car, saying that he must see with his own eyes that the arrangements for the meeting were sound. Hannay was to rest, he said, to eat well and to read any book in the library, and he must on no account leave the grounds. The house seemed suddenly very large and very quiet when the sound of the engine had faded.

Hannay tried to read a novel and found that the print swam before his eyes, and he tried to sleep and found that his mind raced. In the end he gave up and tramped round and round the walled garden like a caged animal, turning over the steps, the tide, the boat and the French general, and he could not make them fit together. All through the long, bright morning of the fifteenth the roses smelled sweet around him, and he was far too anxious to notice.

In London, behind guarded doors, a French general named Royer shook hands that afternoon with a small group of British officers and officials, and the secret meeting began. Everything went smoothly, the papers were signed and sealed, and the general departed as quietly as he had come, and nobody noticed anything amiss. It seemed that the long-feared conspiracy had broken against the vigilance of the guards.

Sir Walter came back late in the afternoon looking weary but pleased, and he reported that the meeting had passed off without the smallest hitch. Hannay, instead of being relieved, grew uneasy and said slowly that this was precisely what the Black Stone would want, for if a thing had been done well enough, nobody would know that anything had been done at all. Sir Walter, who had been about to pour himself a cup of tea, put down the pot and looked at him sharply.

If the spies had been clever enough to copy the plans without a ripple, Hannay argued, they would not linger in England a moment longer than they must, and the boat in Scudder's notes meant tonight. High tide at seventeen minutes past ten, the notebook said, and the clock on the mantelpiece showed that it was nearly five o'clock. There were only five hours left, and they did not even know where to look.

Sir Walter pulled down armfuls of heavy volumes from the library shelves, and for half an hour the two men searched through almanacs, atlases and old yachting guides, flinging aside everything that was no use. At last Sir Walter found a thick, worn volume that listed the times of high water at every harbour and beach round the coast of England. He laid it flat on the table, wiped the dust from the cover with his sleeve and turned the pages with trembling fingers.

Hannay ran his finger down the column of figures for the fifteenth of June, past harbour after harbour, until at last it stopped dead. At a small place called Bradgate, on the coast of Kent, high water was reckoned at seventeen minutes past ten that very night, and no other place on the whole list matched it. Sir Walter breathed out slowly, peered over his spectacles at the page and said quietly that they might at last have found it.

Sir Walter suddenly remembered an old friend who lived scarcely a mile away, a retired naval officer who had spent half his life sailing along the coast of Kent and knew every cove and headland by heart. He sent a car to bring him at once, and the minutes that followed seemed to Hannay to drag like hours. Outside the library window, the long June evening was already beginning to deepen into a soft and dangerous dusk.

In a few minutes the old officer arrived, a brisk, bronzed, white-whiskered man who stumped into the library with a stout stick and a bright, inquisitive eye. He listened eagerly while Sir Walter explained as much as it was safe to say, and then, tugging at his whiskers, he declared that he knew Bradgate like the back of his hand. He had sailed past that stretch of cliff a hundred times, he added, and in all weathers and at all hours.

Bradgate, he said, was a small and sleepy place with a few villas dotted along the top of a high chalk cliff, and a landing beach reached by steep paths and one or two private stairways. One house in particular came to his mind, a white villa called Trafalgar Lodge, whose owner had cut a long wooden stair down the face of the cliff to the sand. He had often admired it from the deck of his old yacht, he said, with the evening sun on its white walls.

At the word stair Hannay leapt to his feet as though he had been stung, for the whole riddle suddenly turned over in his mind and showed its true face. The thirty-nine steps were the steps of the cliff stair at Trafalgar Lodge, he said, and the boat would be waiting at the foot of them when the tide came in at seventeen minutes past ten. Neither of the two old gentlemen could think of a single reason to contradict him, and Sir Walter began to nod slowly.

Without wasting another word, Sir Walter lifted the telephone and called Scotland Yard, and in a clipped, grave voice he asked for a trusted detective named Inspector Scaife. The inspector was to come at once, he said, by the fastest motor car in London and with half a dozen steady men, and he was to breathe a word of his errand to no one. He rang off, glanced at the clock and turned to the others with the air of a general who has given his orders.

Within the hour a large dark motor car swept up the drive, and Inspector Scaife of Scotland Yard stepped into the hall, a broad, quiet man in a bowler hat with shrewd, patient eyes. He looked long and hard at Hannay, whose description he had been carrying in his pocket for three weeks, and then, to the astonishment of everyone, he held out his hand. Sir Walter, it seemed, had already told him a good deal over the telephone.

Scaife listened to the whole story with folded arms and a face like stone, and when it was over he said that it explained a number of things that had puzzled him. There was, for instance, the milkman who had come forward with a strange tale of a gold coin, a joke on some friends and a stranger in a white coat. There was also the knife in the dead man's heart, which had been wiped clean of every mark by someone who knew his business, and he had never quite believed that Hannay was a murderer.

Scaife pointed out that if they arrested the spies too soon, before the plans were in their hands, the evidence might vanish into the sea, so it would be necessary to wait and catch them in the act. He therefore divided his six plain-clothes men between two cars, left strict orders about silence and lights, and prepared to set out. Hannay climbed into the front seat of the first car with a heart that was beating like a drum.
