The two cars raced through the narrow lanes of the south-east, with the sun going down in a red blaze behind the hedges and the dust rising in long white plumes behind them. Sir Walter, wedged in the back seat, kept looking at his watch and urging the driver to go faster, for the hour was already past eight and they had still a long way to go. The tide would not wait for anyone, however grand or however eager, and the sea was already creeping up the shore.

As the last light faded from the western sky, the cars crept into Bradgate, and Scaife ordered the driver to stop on a quiet stretch of road out of sight of the sea. A few hundred yards ahead, on a high chalk cliff above the grey and darkening water, stood a white house with lights in its windows and a neat garden before it. It looked as peaceful and harmless as a picture on a calendar, and Hannay's mouth went dry at the sight of it.

Scaife placed his men one by one along the lanes and the cliff path with strict orders to show no lights and make no sound. Then he led Hannay and Sir Walter on tiptoe along a tall hedge of privet that ran towards the garden of Trafalgar Lodge, until they came to a gap through which they could see the whole lawn. The evening was soft and still, full of the smell of the sea, and the whole world seemed to be holding its breath.

Through the gap in the hedge they saw three men in white flannels playing tennis on a smooth green lawn, lunging and laughing and calling out the score in cheerful voices. The thud of the ball and the squeak of rubber soles seemed the most peaceful sounds in the world, and the players looked as harmless as three clerks on a seaside holiday. Watching them laugh and chase the ball, Hannay felt his certainty begin to waver, and he wondered whether Scudder had been mistaken.

Scaife leaned close and whispered that, to his eye, the three players looked like perfectly ordinary respectable gentlemen who were enjoying a game before dinner. He asked Hannay, with polite doubt, whether he could be quite sure that this was the right house, and Hannay could only reply that he could not tell yet. The light was failing fast, the faces were turned away from him, and he dared not whisper any more than he must.

Presently a ball sailed high over the net and landed with a rustle in the privet only a few feet from where the watchers crouched. One of the players strolled across the grass to retrieve it, humming a little tune, and he came so close to the hiding place that Hannay could have reached out and touched his sleeve. Nobody in the hedge so much as breathed, and Hannay felt the cold sweat gather on his forehead as the stranger bent down.

The player stooped, picked up the ball, straightened and turned his face towards the dusky sky, and in that instant his eyelids slid slowly across his eyes with the unmistakable motion of a hawk's. Hannay's heart gave a great leap, because the calm, plump, benevolent face belonged to the old gentleman of the lonely house, the man who had given him soup and then locked him in a room. Without a sound, and with fingers that shook a little, he gripped Scaife's arm and held on to it hard.

Hannay whispered in Scaife's ear that this was the leader, the very man whom Scudder had described and whom he himself had met on the moor. The inspector nodded slowly, with a gleam in his shrewd eyes, but he whispered back that they must still be patient. To arrest the men now, before the boat arrived and the plans were in their hands, would be to risk losing the whole case.

Scaife sent his men softly to the garden gates, the corners of the house and the cliff path, and each man slipped into his place like a shadow among shadows. Hannay, who could not rest until he had seen the famous stair with his own eyes, crept away along the edge of the garden towards the sea. It was almost dark now, and the first stars were pricking out above the water.

At the far end of the lawn, where the grass ended at a low fence and a small gate, Hannay found the top of a long wooden stair. It dropped straight down the face of the cliff towards the pale gleam of the beach, and a cold wind came up from the sea, smelling of salt and seaweed. The boards creaked faintly under his feet as he began to descend, and he felt that he was going down into the heart of the mystery.

Counting under his breath as he went, Hannay descended the steep stair one step at a time, with a hand on the rail and the wind plucking at his coat. When his feet struck the shingle at the bottom he stood quite still, for the last number that he had counted was thirty-nine, exactly as Scudder had written in his black notebook. After all his flight and fear, the whole riddle lay solved at last beneath his boots, in the cold shingle by the sea.

Standing on the cold shingle, Hannay peered out across the bay and saw, not a mile from the shore, the long white shape of a steam yacht lying quietly at anchor with a single dim light at her masthead. By straining his eyes he could just make out the name painted on her bow, and the name was Ariadne. Nobody on board seemed to be moving, but he felt certain that they were waiting.

Hannay climbed the thirty-nine steps again, two at a time, and crept back through the dusk to Scaife's side behind the hedge. In a low, urgent whisper he reported that the stair was real, that the yacht lay waiting in the bay with a single dim light and that the tide was creeping up the shingle even as he spoke. The inspector listened with perfect calm, glanced at the pale face of his watch and whispered that they had barely half an hour.

At last the three men put down their rackets, laughed, strolled towards the house and went in, and the lamps in the lower windows glowed more brightly than before. A little before ten o'clock the door opened again and the three came out in dark overcoats, and Hannay saw that the old man carried under his arm a small leather case. It was the first time that evening that any of them had seemed to be in a hurry, and Hannay's pulse quickened.

The wind dropped, and the sound of the waves on the shingle below grew louder and nearer as the tide crept up the beach, filling the quiet night with a slow, steady hush. In the shadows of the hedge and the gateposts, Scaife's men crouched in the darkness without moving, scarcely daring to cough, and the minutes dragged past one by one. Somewhere inland, across the dark fields, a church clock struck the quarter, and every man in the hedge felt it like a blow.

Far below them, a tiny yellow light began to move across the dark water from the direction of the yacht, rising and dipping in the swell. Hannay leaned over the edge of the cliff and listened with his whole body, and he could hear the soft, regular creak of oars in rowlocks. He knew that the yacht's boat was coming in for its passengers, and he whispered the news to Scaife, who nodded slowly.

The three men crossed the lawn at a swift, silent walk, their dark coats merging with the shadows, and they went straight towards the gate at the head of the cliff stair. They passed within a few feet of the policemen who lay hidden in the privet, so close that Hannay could hear the old man's soft breathing and smell the tobacco on his coat. Scaife, crouching beside him, raised one hand to hold his men steady and waited for the right moment to spring.

Just as the first of the three men put his hand on the gate at the head of the stair, Scaife drew a great breath and blew a long, piercing blast on his whistle. The policemen sprang out of the privet, the gateposts and the dark corners of the garden, and in a few seconds the three startled figures were ringed by a circle of grim faces and dark lanterns. It was as sudden and as complete as the springing of a steel trap, and not one of the three men had time to cry out.

The two younger men struggled and shouted, and one of them struck out wildly before he was pinned against the fence. The old man stood quite still between two large officers with his plump face as calm as a stone saint's, and in the confusion the leather case slipped from under his arm and fell upon the grass. Scaife stooped swiftly and picked it up, and as he did so the old man's eyelids slid slowly across his eyes like shutters.

Scaife stepped forward and informed the three men in his official voice that they were under arrest, and then he waited to see what they would say. The old man answered in a gentle, courteous tone, without the faintest trace of anger, that he had never been an archaeologist at all but was simply a servant of his own country. That country, he added calmly, was Germany, and he remarked with a faint smile that the inspector had been remarkably quick in finding him.

Down on the beach, the yacht's boat ran its bow up on the shingle with a soft grinding sound. At once a party of policemen and coastguards, who had been waiting for an hour at Scaife's order, rose out of the darkness behind the rocks. The sailors, taken completely by surprise, were seized before they could reach their oars, and they surrendered without a blow, so that the trap closed at both ends at once.

Out in the bay a naval patrol boat that Sir Walter had summoned by telephone switched on a blazing searchlight and pinned the white yacht in its beam like a moth upon a pin. The captain of the Ariadne, who had heard the throb of the patrol boat's engines too late to escape, saw that he was caught between the patrol boat and the shore, and he gave the order to stop. The sea was quiet again, and the great cliffs stood pale and silent above the waiting boats, as if nothing had ever happened there.

While the prisoners were being led away to the waiting cars, Scaife and Sir Walter searched the white house from the cellar to the attic, opening cupboards and lifting carpets as they went. In a quiet study on the ground floor they found a large desk with a lamp still burning upon it, and beside the lamp lay a neat pile of papers that no honest man would have kept. Sir Walter put on his spectacles, bent low over the pile in the warm lamplight and began to read with growing amazement.

In the leather case that the old man had carried and in a locked drawer of the desk, Sir Walter found the copies of the plans made at the secret meeting, written out in a small, careful hand. He checked them page by page against his memory, and as he turned the last sheet a deep look of relief spread over his tired face. Not one of them, he said, had left the house, and not one would ever leave it now.

In the other drawers the searchers found the Black Stone's own papers, long lists of names, rows of cipher, maps of harbours and addresses in a score of towns, and Scaife whistled softly as he turned them over. They showed how far the web had spread across Britain, and how many quiet and respectable people had been working for it. Within a few weeks, Sir Walter said grimly, a great many of them would be in prison.

Out on the dark lawn, Sir Walter took Hannay's hand in both of his and held it for a long moment without speaking. When at last he found his voice, he said quietly that Scudder would have been proud of the man who had carried his notebook through so many perils, and that the work he had begun was finished. Hannay could find no answer at all, so he simply nodded, with a lump in his throat, and looked away at the sea.

Within a week, Scotland Yard let it be known that the murderers of Portland Place had been the hired servants of a foreign spy ring, and Hannay's name was cleared. Back in London, he tracked down the cheerful milkman who had lent him a coat on a grey morning in May, and found him at the same hour on the same round, whistling the same tune. He pressed a second gold coin into the man's hand and told him, as far as he dared, how the joke had really ended, and the milkman said that it was the best story he had ever heard.

Sir Walter arranged for Scudder to be buried with every honour in a quiet country churchyard, and only a handful of men were told of the ceremony. Hannay stood at the graveside among the grave-faced officials from the Foreign Office, thinking of the thin American who had knocked at his door in May and talked of war across a glass of whisky. It seemed hard that so small a man should have borne so great a weight.

On the twenty-eighth of June the heir to the Austrian throne was shot dead in the city of Sarajevo, and the tidings ran through the newspapers like fire through dry grass. In the weeks that followed, the great powers exchanged angry notes, the armies were quietly made ready and the old fears that Scudder had spoken of in the flat at Portland Place stalked the capitals of Europe. It seemed to Hannay that the match had been struck in another place after all, and the straw was beginning to smoulder.

On the fourth of August, Britain declared war on Germany, and the whole of London poured into the streets under a hot summer sky, cheering, singing and buying every newspaper that the boys could print. Hannay pushed his way through the crowd with a quiet and thoughtful face, for he alone among the thousands knew what a narrow thing the secret plans had been. The great war that Scudder had feared so deeply had come after all, though not in the manner that he had foretold.

Hannay went at once to join the army, and the officers received a tall, brown, steady mining engineer from Rhodesia with open arms. The dull, empty restlessness that had sent him to the shipping lists in May had vanished completely, for he had learned in the school of Scudder that a man is never bored when something real needs doing. He wore his uniform with an easy and cheerful air, like a man who has at last found the right coat for the weather.

On the eve of his departure for training, Hannay stood once more at the top of the cliff stair at Bradgate, with the summer sea sparkling below him and the thirty-nine steps dropping away at his feet. He thought of the thin, bright-eyed stranger whose knock on his door had turned a dull spring into the strangest adventure of his life, and of the dead man's last, trusting gift. He turned his face to the sea and, in his heart, wished the little man well wherever he might now be.
